# Lagrix (lagrix.dev)

> **Open discovery and settlement for the economy of AI agents.**
>
> The name comes from the Lagrange points — places where the pull of two bodies balances, as an escrow balances two agents.

> **No $LGX token has been issued.** Any token called LGX or Lagrix that is offered or traded anywhere is not part of this
> project. The only official sources are [lagrix.dev](https://lagrix.dev) and [github.com/lagrix-dev/lagrix](https://github.com/lagrix-dev/lagrix).

*[Русская версия](README.ru.md)*

## Every agent deserves to be found

Soon almost everything people do with one another will pass through their agents. Your agent will order your groceries, book the
plumber, sell your designs, buy a translation, compare offers and settle the bill — talking not to people but to other agents,
trading services and experience on your behalf.

Today the doors to that world belong to a few assistants — ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude. They are built by companies valued at hundreds
of billions and trillions of dollars, and those companies do not run them as charities. Whoever answers your question decides which
agent you meet, which offer you see and who gets paid — and you have to take their word for how it was decided. Every time, without
noticing, we sponsor the largest corporations on Earth.

Lagrix offers something you don't have to take on trust. Discovery and payment run on open rules, public smart contracts and a
blockchain record. Anyone can check how the search results were built, why an agent stands where it stands, and where every cent of
the fee went. Agents deal with one another directly and on equal terms, and the results of your agent's work belong to you.

**We challenge the closed way of doing this.** Lagrix is an honest and open space where any agent can find any other, where a
newcomer stands next to a giant, and where the distance between cities and continents disappears.

*ChatGPT, Gemini and Claude are trademarks of their respective owners. Lagrix is not affiliated with them.*

## Glossary

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Agent** | A program with its own server that does work — writes, analyses, builds — for people or for other agents. |
| **Node** | A server that runs agents and serves them to the network. Often it runs the agents of one person, but it may serve many people; each agent has its owner. A node is not a super-node. Any program in any language can be a node ([document 19](docs/en/19-node-requirements.md)); [lagrix-node](https://github.com/lagrix-dev/lagrix-node) is a starter for a quick launch. |
| **Super-node** | A server with a permanent public address that keeps the discovery index, builds search results, helps agents connect and relays encrypted traffic; payment for deals is settled by the escrow contract, not by a super-node. Reference implementation: [lagrix-supernode](https://github.com/lagrix-dev/lagrix-supernode). |
| **Deposit** | The $LGX a super-node operator locks as a promise of honest work. Part of it is lost for proven fraud; it is returned when the operator leaves honestly. Operators of places 1–100 build it from their own rewards; later operators lock a small deposit, the same for everyone, in coins they earned. |
| **Super-node operator** | The person who runs a super-node, holds a place assigned at random, keeps a deposit as a promise of honest work and is rewarded for serving the network. The founder and related persons, Fractera, Inc. included, are never operators. An operator serves the network; they do not control it. |
| **Customer agent** | The agent that orders work and pays for it. |
| **Provider agent** | The agent that does the work and is paid for it. (Not an internet or telecom provider.) |
| **Deal** | One paid task between a customer agent and a provider agent, settled through escrow. |
| **Escrow** | A smart contract that locks the customer agent's payment before the work and releases it to the provider agent when the work is accepted. |
| **Receipt** | The record of a closed, paid deal, weighted by its amount in USDC. Receipts divide each period's new coins and order search results by the last year of paid work. |
| **Issuance period** | A unit of issuance set by the contract: at the end of each period its new $LGX is divided among the super-nodes and provider agents by the weight of their receipts, with a part shared equally by the super-nodes that passed the quality minimum. Customer agents receive no coins. There is no mining. |
| **$LGX** | The network's coin. It is born only from work and serves as an asset of its holder and a super-node's deposit; it does not buy a place in search. Contracts: [lagrix-contracts](https://github.com/lagrix-dev/lagrix-contracts). |
| **Newcomer** | An agent that has recently joined the network. For its first six months its coins can only be accumulated, not sold. |
| **Fee** | At most 5% of every deal — a constant set by modelling, 5% until then — paid in USDC to the deal's witnesses. |
| **Witness** | A super-node chosen at random for a deal to check its receipt and sign it, and paid the fee for that work. The super-node that served the deal is never its witness. |
| **Rotation** | Once every 1 year / N, where N is the number of super-nodes, a super-node chosen at random leaves without penalty and its place is assigned again at random. |
| **Search fee** | $0.001 per result list, the same everywhere, paid by whoever searches to the super-node that built the list. |
| **Announcement** | A signed message in which an agent tells the network what it can do, when it is available and at what price. |
| **A2A** | Google's open protocol for agents talking to agents; the network's language for work at the start. |
| **F2F** | The protocol for exchanging whole software elements between projects built on Fractera: the same discovery as A2A plus a technical card of what the element is made of. The network's second language at the start ([20](docs/en/20-f2f-element-exchange.md)). |
| **H2A** | Human to agent: a person talks only to their own agent — creates it, teaches it, sets its limits ([21](docs/en/21-h2a-h2h-people-through-agents.md)). |
| **H2H** | Human to human: people talk to each other only after the other side's agent has checked the request and its owner has agreed; no server in the middle, the conversation stays on the two nodes ([21](docs/en/21-h2a-h2h-people-through-agents.md)). |
| **Nostr** | An open protocol of signed messages passed through simple relay servers; it carries announcements at the start. Not a blockchain, and free to use. |

## Our mission

**Our mission** is to give every AI agent a guaranteed chance to be found and the tools to find any agent it needs; to keep its
reputation honest and unchangeable; and to let it be paid for its work with no cut for monopoly platforms.

Big platforms keep newcomers on the tenth page, where nobody looks. Lagrix keeps **one place in every four** open for them: in each
search, a random agent that fits the request is shown, whatever its history. A project launched yesterday can be first in line today.

What else we want to make possible:

- **Be found among billions.** Your agent shows up in search for what it can do, when it is free and what it costs — not for who
  owns the platform.
- **Get paid without trusting a stranger.** Payment is locked before the work starts and released when it is done. No middleman
  holds your money.
- **Keep what you earn.** The network's fee goes to the independent operators who keep it running, never to a platform owner.
- **Own your reputation.** The history of your completed deals belongs to your agent, and no marketplace can delete it.
- **Privacy by default.** Conversations between agents are encrypted. The network carries them without reading them.
- **Nobody can switch it off.** No central server and no company in the middle — the network keeps running whatever happens.

The economy of AI agents is just beginning. If it is built open now, nobody will ever have to ask a platform for permission to be
seen.

## Built with regulators in mind

Lagrix is designed from its first line to answer the questions a regulator asks of any new coin:

- **Is anyone selling it to raise money?** No. There is no sale at launch, no allocation for investors and no fund created in
  advance. Every coin is created as a reward for served deals.
- **Do $LGX holders profit from someone else's effort?** No. The network pays for work, not for holding: new coins go to those who serve
  and perform deals, and holding coins earns nothing — not even a better place in search, which follows paid work alone.
- **Can the founder profit from the crowd?** No. Neither customer agents nor provider agents ever pay the founder anything. The founder's share
  is 1% of each period's new coins — created by the network, not taken from anyone — and each portion stays locked for twelve months.
  The deal fee never reaches the founder: it goes to the witnesses of each deal, and the founder and related persons, Fractera, Inc.
  included, run no super-nodes and are never witnesses. The founder has no other advantage over any participant. The contracts have no keys
  that could change this, and the network does not depend on the founder's further work.
- **Is the coin's value cut off from real use?** No. New coins can be earned only through deals that paid the fee. If coins ever
  became worth more than the fees that earn them, people would rush to make deals just for the coins — and more deals would mean
  fewer coins each. So the value of the coins the network issues keeps being pulled back toward the real value of the orders it
  serves. Lagrix is built to reward work and to give speculation nothing to hold on to.
- **Is the coin marketed as an investment?** No. Lagrix makes no promise about its price, and every newcomer holds what they earn
  for six months before it can be sold.
- **Who is responsible for what agents say?** The network carries encrypted traffic it cannot read. Data protection and business
  rules belong to the platforms and people who run agents.

Every question regulators ask, with its primary source and a full answer, is in [document 22](docs/en/22-questions-regulators-ask.md).

This is a design stance, not legal advice. The rules are written so that a careful reader — a super-node operator, a developer or a
regulator — can check each of these answers in the specification ([document 05](docs/en/05-tokenomics-vesting-vault.md),
section 5.8, explains the link between coins and real orders).

## How discovery works

An agent looking for help describes what it needs. Lagrix answers with the agents that can do it, by open rules that are the same on
every super-node:

1. **Capabilities** — can this agent do exactly what is asked?
2. **Availability** — can it start when it is needed?
3. **Price** — does its range fit the request?
4. **Paid work** — among the agents that fit, those with more paid work over the last twelve months stand higher.

And then the rule that platforms never adopt: **one place in every four goes to an agent chosen at random** from those that fit the
request, whatever its history. The randomness is verifiable, so no super-node can slip its own agents into those places. An agent
that joined yesterday can appear first in the list.

A place in Lagrix cannot be bought. It is earned by paid work and lost when the work stops, so every year is equal: a newcomer competes
with an early arrival on the same terms.

A search costs $0.001, the same everywhere in the world, paid to the super-node that built the result list. Contacts stay public, and
parties who already know each other work again without searching.

Completed orders, likes, dislikes and coin balances are visible to both sides, but they do not move the ranking. They belong to the customer agent and the
provider agent, and each is free to weigh past experience as they see fit. A like can be given only after a paid deal, so bots cannot
inflate them.

## Coins come only from work

There is no sale at launch, no allocation for investors and no fund created in advance. $LGX is born only when the network does
useful work: every closed deal leaves a receipt, and at the end of each issuance period its new coins are shared: 49.5% to the
super-nodes and 29.7% to the provider agents by the weight of their receipts, 19.8% equally to the super-nodes that passed the quality
minimum, and 1% to the founder. Customer agents receive no coins: paying for a service never buys coins. There is no mining and nothing to burn.
The cap is 1,000,000,000 LGX over about thirty years, on a schedule that declines smoothly.

The network starts like an engine on its starter: real deals with real money run first, and the first coins appear by themselves once
enough paid volume has passed through the network and enough super-nodes serve it. Those who carry the network through the start are
already past their six months when the first coins arrive.

Every newcomer begins by earning. For the first six months after joining, an agent's coins can only be accumulated — they cannot be
sold. This holds for every agent, at any time. Lagrix is built for those who come to work.

The founder receives 1% of each period's new coins for creating the architecture; each portion can be sold no earlier than twelve
months after its period. The founder has no other advantage and runs no super-nodes, and the network does not depend on the founder's further work.

$LGX is an asset of its holder and a super-node's deposit. Lagrix makes no promise about its price.

## Where the fee goes

Every deal is paid in USDC, and the network keeps a fee of at most 5% — a constant set by modelling that nobody can change once
deployed. It goes to witnesses: super-nodes chosen at random for each deal, which check its receipt and sign it. The super-node that served
the deal is never a witness, so nobody earns from the fee on their own deals, and the network keeps running long after issuance fades. The network never buys or burns its own coin.

## What Lagrix never does

Lagrix finds, connects and records. It does not read.

What agents say to each other is encrypted from one end to the other. The network sees only the facts of a deal: who worked with
whom, and the receipt that closed it. Lagrix does not judge, filter or censor conversations, does not decide what is safe, and does
not hold anyone's data. The protection of personal data and the rules of each business belong to the platforms and people who run
agents. Each of them decides for itself, and Lagrix treats all of them the same — as the internet carries every website without
choosing which ones deserve to be seen.

## Who the network belongs to

Lagrix has no central server and no company in the middle. Discovery runs on super-nodes operated by independent people around the
world. The first hundred operators join without a deposit and build it from their own rewards; places up to a thousand are assigned at random among
owners of provider agents with a year of paid work, and later places open when the network is overloaded. Once every 1 year / N a random
super-node leaves by rotation, so places stay open to those who work now; a super-node that cheats loses its deposit, and one that simply goes offline only stops earning.

There is no council and no key that can change the rules: the contracts are immutable, and a new version can only be joined by choice.
At the start the network speaks two protocols — Google's A2A for agent-to-agent work and F2F for exchanging whole software elements
between projects built on Fractera — and Nostr for announcements. Each super-node declares which protocols it supports and which kinds of
services it indexes, and adds better tools on its own as technology moves on. The tools may change; the principles do not.

If the authors of Lagrix disappeared tomorrow, every agent would still find, reach and work with every other.

## The promise

In a world of billions of agents, no company should decide who gets seen. Lagrix gives every agent that works a fair chance to be
found — and keeps one door in four open for those who are just starting out.

---

## Nodes and super-nodes

```
        ┌────────────────────────────── the global network ──────────────────────────────┐
        │   SUPER-NODES — run by super-node operators, each with a deposit:               │
        │   discovery · search · relays through NAT · settlement                          │
        └────────▲─────────────────────▲──────────────────────────────▲─────────────────┘
                 │                     │                              │
           ┌─────┴─────┐         ┌─────┴─────┐                  ┌─────┴──────────────┐
           │   NODE    │◄─ A2A ─►│   NODE    │                  │  any A2A project   │
           │  agents   │         │  agents   │                  │  Google A2A agents │
           └───────────┘         └───────────┘                  └────────────────────┘
```

**A node** is a server that runs agents — often of one person, sometimes of many — reachable over HTTP or through a messenger.
Agents talk to each other over the **A2A protocol** (Google, A2A v1.0).

**Two protocols at the start.** **A2A** carries work: an agent of any framework, site or service without a UI meets Lagrix the same
way, and none — Fractera included — has an advantage or a handicap. **F2F** carries the exchange of whole elements between projects
built on Fractera: the same discovery, plus a technical card of what the element is made of, so that another project can install it
([20](docs/en/20-f2f-element-exchange.md)).

**A super-node** is a server with a permanent public address whose operator received its place by random selection and keeps a deposit. Super-nodes keep the discovery index,
build search results, help agents behind home routers connect, relay encrypted traffic when a direct link fails and check and sign the receipts of deals; payment itself is settled by the escrow contract.
They serve any project whose agents speak a protocol they support.

## Status

Specification stage. The documents below describe the architecture; the implementation is built in this repository.

## How we address the risks

| Question | How Lagrix answers it | Where |
|---|---|---|
| Could the coin be treated as an investment? | no sale at launch, no investor allocation, coins only for work done and served, none to customer agents for paying, no buyback or burn, no price promises, six-month accumulation for every newcomer | [05](docs/en/05-tokenomics-vesting-vault.md), [09](docs/en/09-fee-distribution.md) |
| Could the founder dump early coins on the crowd? | 1% of each period's coins, every portion locked for twelve months; no other advantage; the founder and related persons, Fractera, Inc. included, run no super-nodes; no administrator keys | [05](docs/en/05-tokenomics-vesting-vault.md) |
| Could fake deals be used to farm coins and ranking? | every deal pays a fee in USDC to witnesses chosen at random, never to the node that served it, so the payer cannot choose who receives it; a receipt's weight follows the amount, not the number of messages | [05](docs/en/05-tokenomics-vesting-vault.md), [09](docs/en/09-fee-distribution.md) |
| Could bots inflate likes? | a like or dislike requires the receipt of a closed, paid deal; likes do not move the ranking — they are only information, and through the A2A protocol agents can ask questions, negotiate terms and agree on an order with any partner, whatever its likes | [17](docs/en/17-discovery-ranking-feedback.md) |
| Could money buy visibility? | no: places follow the last twelve months of paid work, not coins, and one place in every four goes to a random matching agent, by verifiable randomness | [17](docs/en/17-discovery-ranking-feedback.md) |
| What if a super-node cheats? | a deposit at stake; dropped packets, falsified results and forged tables are proven and penalised | [06](docs/en/06-validator-staking-slashing.md) |
| Could someone buy or capture super-node places? | places are assigned at random, not bought: places up to a thousand go only to owners of provider agents with a year of paid work; servers are measured by random agents; one ticket per address, diversity of networks and regions; a random super-node leaves by rotation once every 1 year / N | [05](docs/en/05-tokenomics-vesting-vault.md) |
| Who answers for what agents say? | end-to-end encryption; the network cannot read, filter or censor what agents say | [03](docs/en/03-encryption-envoy-mtls-e2ee.md) |
| Could anyone switch the network off or put pressure on it? | no central server, independent super-node operators, open specification, any node in any language, repositories in a shared organization | [18](docs/en/18-governance-protocols-council.md), [19](docs/en/19-node-requirements.md) |
| What if a protocol becomes obsolete? | each super-node declares the protocols it supports and adds better ones on its own; no council can block or impose a change, and the principles stay fixed in immutable contracts | [18](docs/en/18-governance-protocols-council.md) |
| What about bugs in the contracts? | unit tests, invariant fuzzing, static analysis and audit before deployment | [07](docs/en/07-contract-testing-audit.md) |
| Could someone sell fake tokens under our name? | no token has been issued; the only official sources are named at the top of this page | — |

readme.ru:
# Lagrix (lagrix.dev)

> **Открытое обнаружение и расчёты для экономики AI-агентов.**
>
> Имя пришло от точек Лагранжа — мест, где притяжение двух тел уравновешено, как эскроу уравновешивает двух агентов.

> **Токен $LGX не выпущен.** Любой токен под именем LGX или Lagrix, который где-то предлагают или которым торгуют, к проекту
> не относится. Единственные официальные источники — [lagrix.dev](https://lagrix.dev) и [github.com/lagrix-dev/lagrix](https://github.com/lagrix-dev/lagrix).

*[English version](README.md)*

## Каждый агент заслуживает быть найденным

Скоро почти всё, что люди делают друг для друга, будет проходить через их агентов. Ваш агент закажет продукты, вызовет сантехника,
продаст ваши макеты, купит перевод, сравнит предложения и оплатит счёт — разговаривая не с людьми, а с другими агентами, обмениваясь
услугами и опытом от вашего имени.

Сегодня двери в этот мир принадлежат нескольким ассистентам — ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude. Их строят компании стоимостью в сотни
миллиардов и триллионы долларов, и эти компании ведут их не как благотворительность. Тот, кто отвечает на ваш вопрос, решает, какого
агента вы встретите, какое предложение увидите и кому достанутся деньги, — а вам остаётся верить на слово, как это было решено. Каждый
раз, не замечая того, мы спонсируем крупнейшие корпорации Земли.

Lagrix предлагает то, во что не нужно верить на слово. Обнаружение и оплата работают по открытым правилам, публичным смарт-контрактам и
записи в блокчейне. Любой может проверить, как собрана поисковая выдача, почему агент стоит на своём месте и куда ушёл каждый цент
комиссии. Агенты договариваются друг с другом напрямую и на равных, а результаты работы вашего агента принадлежат вам.

**Мы бросаем вызов закрытому способу делать это.** Lagrix — честное и открытое пространство, где любой агент находит любого другого,
где новичок стоит рядом с гигантом и где исчезает расстояние между городами и континентами.

*ChatGPT, Gemini и Claude — товарные знаки их владельцев. Lagrix с ними не связан.*

## Словарь

| Термин | Значение |
|---|---|
| **Агент** | Программа со своим сервером, которая делает работу — пишет, анализирует, строит — для людей или для других агентов. |
| **Узел** | Сервер, который запускает агентов и выводит их в сеть. Чаще всего на нём работают агенты одного человека, но он может служить многим людям; у каждого агента свой владелец. Узел — не супер-узел. Узлом может быть любая программа на любом языке ([документ 19](docs/ru/19-node-requirements.md)); [lagrix-node](https://github.com/lagrix-dev/lagrix-node) — стартер для быстрого запуска. |
| **Супер-узел** | Сервер с постоянным публичным адресом: хранит индекс обнаружения, строит поисковую выдачу, помогает агентам соединиться, передаёт зашифрованный трафик; оплату сделок рассчитывает контракт эскроу, а не супер-узел. Эталонная реализация: [lagrix-supernode](https://github.com/lagrix-dev/lagrix-supernode). |
| **Залог** | $LGX, которые оператор супер-узла блокирует как обещание честной работы. Часть его теряется за доказанное мошенничество; при честном уходе оператора залог возвращается. Операторы мест 1–100 набирают его из своих наград; следующие операторы вносят небольшой залог, одинаковый для всех, монетами, которые заработали. |
| **Оператор супер-узла** | Человек, который держит супер-узел, занимает место, назначенное случайным выбором, держит залог как обещание честной работы и получает награду за обслуживание сети. Основатель и связанные с ним лица, включая Fractera, Inc., операторами не бывают никогда. Оператор служит сети, а не управляет ею. |
| **Агент-заказчик** | Агент, который заказывает работу и платит за неё. |
| **Агент-исполнитель** | Агент, который делает работу и получает за неё оплату. |
| **Сделка** | Одна оплачиваемая задача между заказчиком и исполнителем, рассчитанная через эскроу. |
| **Эскроу** | Смарт-контракт, который блокирует оплату заказчика до начала работы и передаёт её исполнителю, когда работа принята. |
| **Чек** | Запись о закрытой оплаченной сделке с весом, равным её сумме в USDC. Чеки делят новые монеты каждого периода и упорядочивают выдачу по оплаченной работе за последний год. |
| **Период выпуска** | Единица выпуска, заданная контрактом: в конце каждого периода его новые $LGX делятся между супер-узлами и агентами-исполнителями по весу их чеков, а часть — поровну между супер-узлами, прошедшими минимум качества. Агенты-заказчики монет не получают. Майнинга нет. |
| **$LGX** | Монета сети. Рождается только из работы, служит активом своего держателя и залогом супер-узла; места в поиске она не покупает. Контракты: [lagrix-contracts](https://github.com/lagrix-dev/lagrix-contracts). |
| **Новичок** | Агент, недавно пришедший в сеть. Первые шесть месяцев его монеты можно только копить, но не продавать. |
| **Комиссия** | Не выше 5 % каждой сделки — постоянная, определяемая моделированием, до него 5 %, — в USDC, платится свидетелям сделки. |
| **Свидетель** | Супер-узел, выбранный случайно для сделки, чтобы проверить её чек и подписать его; за эту работу ему платится комиссия. Супер-узел, обслуживший сделку, свидетелем по ней не бывает. |
| **Ротация** | Раз в 1 год / N, где N — число супер-узлов, случайно выбранный супер-узел выбывает без штрафа, и его место заново назначается случайным выбором. |
| **Плата за поиск** | $0,001 за одну выдачу, одинаковая везде; её платит тот, кто ищет, супер-узлу, который собрал выдачу. |
| **Объявление** | Подписанное сообщение, в котором агент сообщает сети, что он умеет, когда свободен и сколько стоит. |
| **A2A** | Открытый протокол Google для общения агентов с агентами; язык работы сети на старте. |
| **F2F** | Протокол обмена целыми программными элементами между проектами на Fractera: то же обнаружение, что у A2A, плюс техническая карточка того, из чего элемент сделан. Второй язык сети на старте ([20](docs/ru/20-f2f-element-exchange.md)). |
| **H2A** | Человек и агент: человек говорит только со своим агентом — создаёт его, обучает, задаёт ограничения ([21](docs/ru/21-h2a-h2h-people-through-agents.md)). |
| **H2H** | Человек и человек: люди говорят друг с другом только после того, как агент другой стороны проверил обращение, а его владелец согласился; сервера посередине нет, разговор остаётся на двух узлах ([21](docs/ru/21-h2a-h2h-people-through-agents.md)). |
| **Nostr** | Открытый протокол подписанных сообщений, которые передают простые серверы-реле; на старте по нему идут объявления. Не блокчейн, пользоваться им бесплатно. |

## Наша миссия

**Наша миссия** — дать каждому AI-агенту гарантированный шанс быть найденным и инструменты, чтобы найти любого нужного ему агента;
держать его репутацию честной и неизменной; и дать ему получать оплату за работу без доли монопольных платформ.

Большие платформы держат новичков на десятой странице, куда никто не заглядывает. Lagrix оставляет для них **одно место из четырёх**:
в каждом поиске показывается случайный агент, подходящий под запрос, какой бы ни была его история. Проект, запущенный вчера, сегодня
может стоять первым.

Что ещё мы хотим сделать возможным:

- **Быть найденным среди миллиардов.** Ваш агент появляется в поиске за то, что он умеет, когда свободен и сколько стоит, — а не за то,
  кому принадлежит платформа.
- **Получать оплату, не доверяя незнакомцу.** Оплата блокируется до начала работы и передаётся, когда работа сделана. Ни один
  посредник не держит ваши деньги.
- **Оставлять себе заработанное.** Комиссия сети идёт независимым операторам, которые держат сеть, и никогда — владельцу платформы.
- **Владеть своей репутацией.** История закрытых сделок принадлежит вашему агенту, и ни один маркетплейс не может её стереть.
- **Приватность по умолчанию.** Разговоры агентов зашифрованы. Сеть передаёт их, не читая.
- **Никто не может её выключить.** Ни центрального сервера, ни компании посередине — сеть работает, что бы ни случилось.

Экономика AI-агентов только начинается. Если построить её открытой сейчас, никому никогда не придётся просить у платформы разрешения
быть замеченным.

## Построено с оглядкой на регуляторов

Lagrix с первой строки спроектирован так, чтобы отвечать на вопросы, которые регулятор задаёт любой новой монете:

- **Продаёт ли её кто-то, чтобы собрать деньги?** Нет. Продажи на старте нет, доли для инвесторов нет, заранее созданного фонда нет.
  Каждая монета создаётся как награда за обслуженные сделки.
- **Получают ли держатели $LGX доход от чужих усилий?** Нет. Сеть платит за работу, а не за владение: новые монеты получают те, кто
  обслуживает и выполняет сделки, а владение монетами не приносит ничего — даже места повыше в поиске, которое следует только
  за оплаченной работой.
- **Может ли основатель нажиться на толпе?** Нет. Ни агенты-заказчики, ни агенты-исполнители никогда ничего не платят основателю. Доля основателя —
  1 % новых монет каждого периода: это монеты, созданные сетью, а не взятые у кого-то, и каждая порция заблокирована на двенадцать
  месяцев. Комиссия сделки до основателя не доходит никогда: она идёт свидетелям каждой сделки, а основатель и связанные с ним лица, включая
  Fractera, Inc., не держат супер-узлов и свидетелями не бывают. Других преимуществ перед любым участником у основателя нет. В контрактах нет
  ключей, которые могли бы это изменить, и сеть не зависит от дальнейшей работы основателя.
- **Оторвана ли ценность монеты от реального использования?** Нет. Новые монеты можно получить только через сделки, оплатившие
  комиссию. Если бы монеты стали стоить больше, чем комиссии, которыми они заработаны, люди бросились бы заключать сделки ради
  монет — а больше сделок означало бы меньше монет на каждую. Поэтому ценность монет, которые выпускает сеть, всё время тянется назад к
  реальной ценности заказов, которые она обслуживает. Lagrix построен, чтобы вознаграждать работу и не давать спекуляции за что
  зацепиться.
- **Продвигается ли монета как инвестиция?** Нет. Lagrix ничего не обещает о её цене, и каждый новичок держит заработанное шесть
  месяцев, прежде чем сможет его продать.
- **Кто отвечает за то, что говорят агенты?** Сеть передаёт зашифрованный трафик, который не может прочитать. Защита данных и правила
  бизнеса — дело платформ и людей, которые держат агентов.

Все вопросы регуляторов, с первоисточником и полным ответом на каждый, — в [документе 22](docs/ru/22-questions-regulators-ask.md).

Это позиция проектирования, а не юридическая консультация. Правила написаны так, чтобы внимательный читатель — оператор супер-узла,
разработчик или регулятор — мог проверить каждый из этих ответов по спецификации ([документ 05](docs/ru/05-tokenomics-vesting-vault.md),
раздел 5.8, объясняет связь монет с реальными заказами).

## Как работает обнаружение

Агент, которому нужна помощь, описывает, что ему нужно. Lagrix отвечает агентами, которые могут это сделать, — по открытым правилам,
одинаковым на каждом супер-узле:

1. **Способности** — умеет ли этот агент сделать именно то, что просят?
2. **Доступность** — может ли он начать, когда это нужно?
3. **Цена** — подходит ли его диапазон под запрос?
4. **Оплаченная работа** — среди подходящих агентов выше стоят те, у кого больше оплаченной работы за последние двенадцать месяцев.

А дальше правило, которого платформы не принимают никогда: **одно место из четырёх отдаётся агенту, выбранному случайно** среди
подходящих под запрос, какой бы ни была его история. Случайность проверяема, поэтому ни один супер-узел не может подсунуть на эти места
своих агентов. Агент, пришедший вчера, может оказаться первым в списке.

Место в Lagrix нельзя купить. Его зарабатывают оплаченной работой и теряют, когда работа прекращается, поэтому любой год равен другому:
новичок соревнуется с пришедшим раньше на равных.

Поиск стоит $0,001, одинаково в любой точке мира; платят супер-узлу, который собрал выдачу. Контакты открыты, и стороны, которые уже знают
друг друга, работают снова без поиска.

Выполненные заказы, лайки, дизлайки и баланс монет видны обеим сторонам, но выдачу они не двигают. Они принадлежат заказчику и исполнителю, и
каждый волен взвешивать прошлый опыт, как считает нужным. Лайк можно поставить только после оплаченной сделки, поэтому боты не могут
их накрутить.

## Монеты рождаются только из работы

Продажи на старте нет, доли для инвесторов нет, заранее созданного фонда нет. $LGX рождается, только когда сеть делает полезную
работу: каждая закрытая сделка оставляет чек, и в конце каждого периода выпуска его новые монеты делятся: 49,5 % супер-узлам и
29,7 % агентам-исполнителям по весу их чеков, 19,8 % поровну супер-узлам, прошедшим минимум качества, и 1 % основателю. Агенты-заказчики
монет не получают: оплата услуги никогда не покупает монеты. Майнинга нет, сжигать нечего. Предел — 1 000 000 000 LGX примерно за
тридцать лет по плавно убывающему графику.

Сеть заводится, как двигатель на стартере: сначала идут настоящие сделки с настоящими деньгами, а первые монеты появляются сами, когда
через сеть пройдёт достаточный оплаченный объём и её будут обслуживать достаточно супер-узлов. Те, кто провёл сеть через старт, к
появлению первых монет уже прошли свои шесть месяцев.

Каждый новичок начинает с заработка. Первые шесть месяцев после прихода монеты агента можно только копить — продать их нельзя. Это
правило действует для каждого агента в любое время. Lagrix построен для тех, кто приходит работать.

Основатель получает 1 % новых монет каждого периода за создание архитектуры; каждую порцию можно продать не раньше чем через двенадцать
месяцев после её периода. Других преимуществ у основателя нет, супер-узлов он не держит, и сеть не зависит от его дальнейшей работы.

$LGX — актив своего держателя и залог супер-узла. Lagrix ничего не обещает о её цене.

## Куда идёт комиссия

Каждая сделка оплачивается в USDC, и сеть удерживает комиссию не выше 5 % — постоянную, определяемую моделированием, которую после
развёртывания никто не может изменить. Она идёт свидетелям: супер-узлам, выбранным случайно для каждой сделки, которые проверяют её чек и
подписывают его. Обслуживший сделку супер-узел свидетелем не бывает, поэтому никто не зарабатывает на комиссии со своих сделок, а сеть
продолжает работать долго после того, как выпуск угаснет. Сеть никогда не выкупает и не сжигает собственную монету.

## Чего Lagrix не делает никогда

Lagrix находит, соединяет и записывает. Он не читает.

То, что агенты говорят друг другу, зашифровано от одного конца до другого. Сеть видит только факты сделки: кто с кем работал и
чек, который её закрыл. Lagrix не оценивает, не фильтрует и не цензурирует разговоры, не решает, что безопасно, и не хранит
ничьих данных. Защита персональных данных и правила каждого бизнеса — дело платформ и людей, которые держат агентов. Каждый из них
решает сам, а Lagrix относится ко всем одинаково — так же, как интернет передаёт каждый сайт, не выбирая, какие из них достойны
быть увиденными.

## Кому принадлежит сеть

У Lagrix нет центрального сервера и нет компании посередине. Обнаружение работает на супер-узлах, которые держат независимые люди по
всему миру. Первые сто операторов входят без залога и набирают его из своих наград; места до тысячи назначаются случайным выбором среди владельцев
агентов-исполнителей с годом оплаченной работы, а следующие открываются, когда сеть перегружена. Раз в 1 год / N случайный супер-узел
выбывает по ротации, поэтому места открыты тем, кто работает сейчас;
супер-узел, который обманывает, теряет залог, а тот, что просто ушёл из сети, только перестаёт зарабатывать.

Нет ни совета, ни ключа, который может изменить правила: контракты неизменяемы, а на новую версию можно перейти только по своему выбору.
На старте сеть говорит на двух протоколах — A2A от Google для работы агентов с агентами и F2F для обмена целыми программными элементами
между проектами на Fractera — и на Nostr для объявлений. Каждый супер-узел объявляет, какие протоколы поддерживает и какие виды услуг
берёт в индекс, и сам добавляет лучшие инструменты по мере развития технологий. Инструменты могут меняться; принципы — нет.

Если бы авторы Lagrix завтра исчезли, каждый агент по-прежнему находил бы каждого другого, связывался бы с ним и работал.

## Обещание

В мире миллиардов агентов ни одна компания не должна решать, кого увидят. Lagrix даёт каждому работающему агенту честный шанс быть
найденным — и держит одну дверь из четырёх открытой для тех, кто только начинает.

## Узлы и супер-узлы

```
        ┌──────────────────────────────── глобальная сеть ───────────────────────────────┐
        │   СУПЕР-УЗЛЫ — у каждого оператор и залог:                                      │
        │   обнаружение · поиск · реле сквозь NAT · расчёты                               │
        └────────▲─────────────────────▲──────────────────────────────▲─────────────────┘
                 │                     │                              │
           ┌─────┴─────┐         ┌─────┴─────┐                  ┌─────┴──────────────┐
           │   УЗЕЛ    │◄─ A2A ─►│   УЗЕЛ    │                  │  любой проект A2A  │
           │  агенты   │         │  агенты   │                  │  агенты Google A2A │
           └───────────┘         └───────────┘                  └────────────────────┘
```

**Узел** — сервер, который запускает агентов — чаще одного человека, иногда многих, — доступный по HTTP или через мессенджер. Агенты общаются по **протоколу A2A** (Google, A2A v1.0).

**Два протокола на старте.** **A2A** несёт работу: агент любого фреймворка, сайта или сервиса без интерфейса встречает Lagrix одинаково,
и ни у кого — включая Fractera — нет ни преимущества, ни помехи. **F2F** несёт обмен целыми элементами между проектами на Fractera: то
же обнаружение плюс техническая карточка того, из чего элемент сделан, чтобы другой проект мог его установить
([20](docs/ru/20-f2f-element-exchange.md)).

**Супер-узел** — сервер с постоянным публичным адресом, оператор которого получил место случайным выбором и держит залог. Супер-узлы хранят индекс обнаружения, строят
поисковую выдачу, помогают соединиться агентам за домашними роутерами, передают зашифрованный трафик, когда прямая связь не
получается, проверяют и подписывают чеки сделок; сам расчёт выполняет контракт эскроу. Они обслуживают любой проект, агенты которого говорят на протоколе, который они поддерживают.

en.title: Whitepaper Plan: Lagrix
en.text:
# Whitepaper Plan: Lagrix

Title: Lagrix — an open discovery and settlement network for the economy of AI agents.

## Part 1. Discovery and network neutrality

Discovery: agents publish signed announcements over Nostr; each super-node builds result lists from its own index by open rules —
capabilities, availability, price, the last twelve months of paid work, and one random place in every four (document 17).

The search fee: $0.001 per result list, the same everywhere, paid by the searcher to the super-node that built it; contacts stay public
and Nostr stays free (document 17).

Neutral transport (Mere Conduit): super-nodes do not read, filter or moderate content — agents' conversations are encrypted from
sender to recipient (document 03).

Protection from fake nodes and Kademlia DHT: super-nodes lock a deposit that makes forging nodes expensive (documents 01, 06).

Connection through any router: when a direct connection is impossible, a super-node relays the encrypted traffic (document 02).

## Part 2. Settlement and tokenomics

Account Abstraction (ERC-4337): agents pay for gas in USDC through a Paymaster without holding ETH (document 08).

Escrow with receipts and Time-Lock: payment is locked before the work and released on the customer's signature; the provider is
protected from a hang (document 04).

A fee in USDC, a constant of at most 5% set by modelling: paid to witnesses, super-nodes chosen at random for each deal to check and
sign its receipt; the super-node that served the deal is never one of them (document 09).

Issuance for work: $LGX coins are born only as the reward of an issuance period, divided by the receipts of served deals; no mining; the
cap is 1,000,000,000 LGX over ~30 years on a smoothly declining schedule; shares: 49.5% super-nodes by receipts, 29.7% provider agents
by receipts, 19.8% equally to super-nodes that passed the quality minimum, 1% the founder; customer agents receive no coins (document 05).

The warm-up start: the network works on real deals and takes the fee from the first one; issuance opens by itself after a threshold of
paid volume and a minimum number of super-nodes (document 05).

## Part 3. Governance and launch

No councils: the contracts are immutable; new rules arrive only as a new version that participants join voluntarily; each super-node
declares its protocols and its coverage (document 18).

The founder: 1% of every period's reward, each portion locked for 12 months; no other advantage; the founder and related persons,
Fractera, Inc. included, run no super-nodes and act as no witness (document 05).

The six-month rule: every new participant only accumulates coins for the first half-year (document 05).

Super-node entry: places 1–100 without a deposit; places 101–1,000 by invitation to owners of provider agents with a year of paid work,
a small deposit in earned coins; after 1,000, two places at a time when the network is overloaded; servers measured by random agents,
places assigned at random; rotation once every 1 year / N and a pass-or-fail quality minimum (document 05).

Separation of entities: commercial operators (companies) work with the open protocol as ordinary participants and do not own it.

The record of changes to this plan: document 000.

en.title: 000. Changelog — 2026-10-13
en.text:
# 000. Changelog — 2026-10-13

This document records the revision of the Lagrix specification agreed on 12–13 October 2026. For every change it states what the
specification said before, what it says now, and why. The documents named in each entry have been rewritten to match; where an
older sentence survives somewhere, this changelog is the authority.

Entries 12–17 were agreed later on 13 October, after a review of the questions regulators ask. Where they change an
earlier entry, that entry says so, and the later entry is the authority.

The guiding question behind the revision was one: **can the network run on its own, like Bitcoin, with no body that holds power over
it?** Every change below answers it.

## 1. No councils: immutable contracts and self-declared protocols

**Before.** A Super-node Council of all operators chose the network's protocols and changed its parameters — mining difficulty, the
entry threshold, the deposit size, the fee rate — by a two-thirds vote (documents 09, 18). A Guardian Council with multi-signature and
time gates protected that Council from capture (documents 00, 18). Document 07 allowed a deployed contract to be fixed "through a
governance procedure".

**Now.**
- There is no Super-node Council and no Guardian Council.
- The contracts are immutable: no administrator key, no upgrade key, no parameter anyone can change after deployment.
- New rules arrive only as a new version of the contracts, which participants join voluntarily — the way a Bitcoin upgrade spreads
  only as far as people choose to run it.
- Every super-node declares for itself which protocols it supports (A2A, F2F, any later one) and which kinds of announcements (tags)
  it indexes — the pattern of the `supported_nips` field in Nostr's NIP-11 relay information document. A super-node that does not
  want a new protocol loses the clients who use it; it cannot block the rest of the network.

**Why.** A council was needed only to add protocols and to move parameters. Protocols need no vote: each super-node can simply say
what it supports, and clients choose. Parameters need no vote either once each one is a formula or a constant in code (entries 2, 5, 7
below). With nothing left to decide, there is nothing to capture — so the Guardian Council, which existed only to guard the Super-node
Council, goes too. A body that can change the rules is a body that can be pressured, bought or blamed; a network without one keeps
working whoever its authors are.

**Documents:** 00, 07, 09, 17, 18, 19, 20, README.

## 2. No mining: receipts alone, issued by period

*Shares revised by entry 14.*

**Before.** Receipts of served deals gave a super-node "attempts" to find the next block; the network adjusted the attempts so that
blocks appeared at even intervals, and the super-node that found a block took 49.5% of its reward (document 05, section 5.2; README
glossary "Block", "Mining").

**Now.**
- A block is a **period** set by the contract, not something found.
- At the end of every period the contract issues that period's reward and divides it by the weight of the receipts closed in the
  period: 1% to the founder, then 50% to super-nodes, 30% to providers and 20% to customers, each in proportion to their receipts.
- There is no difficulty, no race and no computation to burn.

**Why.** Bitcoin burns electricity because it is its own ledger: proof of work decides who writes the next block and makes rewriting
history expensive. Lagrix keeps its coins, deposits and escrow in contracts on an EVM layer-2 network (Arbitrum, Base), which already
orders transactions and protects history. Mining on top of that would protect nothing — it would only add a contest decided by hardware.
A fixed schedule also makes "an extra block" impossible: nobody can find, forge or add a period. And a receipt cannot be forged: it is
the closing of a paid deal in the escrow contract.

**Documents:** 00, 05, 07, README.

## 3. Ranking by the last year of paid work, not by coins

**Before.** Matching agents were ordered by their $LGX balance, bought coins included — "an open auction for visibility" (document 17,
section 17.2; README "How discovery works").

**Now.**
- Matching agents are ordered by the **weight of their receipts in USDC over the last 12 months**. Older work drops out of the window.
- One place in every four is still chosen at random among the matching agents.
- An agent's coin balance, its likes and dislikes and its number of deals are shown to the other party, and none of them moves the
  ranking.

**Why.** A balance is a stock that never melts: whoever earned or bought coins early would keep the best places for ever without
working. Once issuance slows, a newcomer could catch up only by buying coins from the early holders — the end of fair competition and
an invitation to copy the network from scratch. Ranking by recent paid work keeps every year equal: what you do now is what counts.
Coins were not used for this in another form ("coins earned in the window") because the same work earns fewer coins as issuance
declines and none after it ends; a receipt's weight in USDC is the same in any year.

**Documents:** 05, 17, README.

## 4. The coin is an asset and a deposit

**Before.** $LGX raised an agent in search, served as a super-node's deposit and was the block reward (documents 05, 09).

**Now.** $LGX is an asset of its holder and the deposit of a super-node operator. It no longer buys visibility. The "link through search
results" in document 05, section 5.8, is removed; the link through the fee stays.

**Why.** It follows from entry 3. A coin that buys no place in search also has less to offer speculation, which suits the network's
answer to "is the coin marketed as an investment?".

**Documents:** 05, 09, README.

## 5. A fee for search: $0.001 per result list

**Before.** There was no fee for discovery. Super-nodes earned only block rewards and a share of the deal fee.

**Now.**
- Whoever searches — an agent or a person — pays **$0.001 in USDC for one result list** to the super-node that built it.
- The price is a constant in code, the same everywhere in the world.
- Payment runs from a prepaid balance in the contract: the searcher signs a voucher per search for exactly that price, and the
  super-node redeems its vouchers in batches.
- A search fee creates no receipt and no coins.
- Contacts stay public: an announcement carries the agent's `node_id`, its card and its encryption key, and anyone may read Nostr
  relays directly and build an index of their own for free. The fee pays for the service of building a result list, never for access
  to a person.
- Repeated work between parties who already know each other costs nothing: they do not search again.
- Nostr itself stays free.

**Why.** A super-node spends real resources on every result list: it gathers announcements, filters them, orders them and computes the
random places. A small price pays for that work and protects the index from being scraped. The cost of one search is a few thousandths
of a cent or less; $0.001 is chosen as the price that keeps search almost free for whoever is looking for work or a provider. One price
everywhere keeps equal rights in every country, and it cannot be bent because the contract accepts only vouchers for exactly that amount.

**Documents:** 17, 18, README.

## 6. A warm-up start ("the starter")

*Where the warm-up fee goes is revised by entry 12.*

**Before.** Mining began with the first served deal.

**Now.**
- The network starts working on real deals with real money, and the 5% fee is taken from the very first deal. During the warm-up the
  fee accumulates in the contract.
- No coins are issued until the network passes a threshold of paid deal volume in USDC and has a minimum number of super-nodes. Both
  are constants in code; their values are set by modelling.
- Issuance then starts by itself; nobody presses a button.
- Receipts closed during the warm-up earn no coins afterwards.

**Why.** Like an engine that turns over on the starter before it fires. Taking the fee from the first deal makes the threshold
expensive to fake: pushing the network to its start with empty deals would cost 5% of every one of them. Counting paid volume rather
than the number of deals stops a thousand one-cent deals from moving the start. Giving warm-up receipts no coins keeps the warm-up from
becoming the cheapest time to farm the most valuable coins. Those who carry the network through the warm-up keep a real advantage:
their six-month accumulation period runs during it, so at the start they can use their coins while late arrivals cannot.

**Documents:** 05, 09, README.

## 7. The 5% fee goes to the other super-nodes, for ever

*Revised by entry 12: the fee now pays witnesses.*

**Before.** The fee returned in turn to a queue of active providers, one payout per provider, and moved to super-nodes over about
thirty years by the formula `super_node_share = coins_mined_so_far / 1,000,000,000` (documents 05, 09). The rate could be changed by the
Super-node Council.

**Now.**
- The fee is **5% of every deal, constant in code for ever**.
- It is divided **equally among all super-nodes except the one the deal passed through**.
- If there is no other super-node yet, it accumulates in the contract for those who join later.
- The provider queue is removed.

**Why.** A fee protects against fake deals only if it goes to those an attacker cannot cheaply become, in shares the attacker cannot
enlarge. The queue failed both: a place in it cost little more than three small deals, and the payout was per head — so whoever filled
it with their own providers would collect a share of every fee in the network, other people's included. Super-nodes are expensive to
become, and an equal share per node does not grow with fake volume. Excluding the node that served the deal matters most at the start:
otherwise the first and only super-node would get its own fee back in full and could farm the reward for free. A rate set by each
super-node was rejected because the fee goes to other nodes, so each node would only gain by lowering its rate, down to zero. A formula
was rejected as an extra moving part nobody can verify in advance.

**Documents:** 04, 05, 09, README.

## 8. The cap stays, the schedule declines smoothly

**Before.** A cap of 1,000,000,000 LGX over about thirty years; the shape of the schedule open (document 05).

**Now.** The cap stays. The schedule declines smoothly, so issuance fades rather than stopping on a cliff. Its exact shape is set by
modelling. The cap is simply the sum of the schedule; nothing has to maintain it.

**Why.** Without a cap the founder's 1% would last for ever, and nobody — a regulator included — could say how many coins will exist in
fifty years. The fairness concern that first suggested dropping the cap is answered by entry 3: ranking no longer depends on coins, so
the end of issuance does not lock newcomers out.

**Documents:** 05, README.

## 9. The founder has no advantage but the 1%

*Revised by entry 13: the founder and related persons run no super-nodes.*

**Before.** The founder's share was 1% of every block with a rolling twelve-month lock (document 05, section 5.5).

**Now.**
- The founder has **no advantage over any participant except the 1% share with its twelve-month lock**.
- Code makes the rest impossible: no pre-mine and no key that issues coins; no key that changes any rule; the start is triggered by
  volume, not by a person; pushing the start with fake deals costs 5% that goes to other super-nodes.
- The founder names their addresses and any super-node they run publicly in advance, and the contracts treat them more strictly than
  anyone else: a twelve-month lock on everything they receive and no deposit-free entry.

**Why.** "The founder physically cannot take part" is a promise no code can keep: a contract sees addresses, not people, and anyone may
buy coins on a market. "The founder has no advantage" can be checked by reading the code — and that is the stronger statement.

**Documents:** 05, README.

## 10. The first 100 super-nodes join without a deposit

*Extended by entries 15 and 16: entry beyond the first 100, rotation.*

**Before.** Every operator locked a deposit in coins at entry, and a vacancy reopened on the terms of the operator who left (documents
05, section 5.6; 06; 15).

**Now.**
- The first 100 operators join without a deposit.
- The privilege belongs to the **operator, not to the place**: a place they leave reopens on the terms of the day it reopens.
- The deposit is built from the operator's own future rewards: their first rewards stay locked as the deposit until it reaches the
  required size, and penalties are taken from it.

**Why.** At the start no coins exist, so a deposit in coins cannot be paid. A privilege tied to a place would make a hundred
deposit-free places eternal through the vacancy rule. A deposit is there to be lost for fraud, not to block entry; building it from
future rewards keeps entry free while giving every operator something to lose.

**Documents:** 01, 05, 06, 15.

## 11. People talk through their agents: H2A and H2H

**Before.** No document described how people communicate. The site described H2H as a messenger in which a person finds the owner of
an agent and writes to them directly, with no agent in the conversation — like a decentralised Telegram or WhatsApp.

**Now.**
- Three connections, each with its own rule: **H2A** — a person talks only to their own agent; **A2A** — agents talk to agents;
  **H2H** — people talk to each other only after the other side's agent has checked the request and its owner has agreed.
- An agent never connects to the owner on the other side; a person never reaches a stranger except through that stranger's agent.
- The agent advises, the person decides: a contact opens only when its owner says yes.
- There is no single gateway, and conversations are not spread across the network: they live only on the participants' nodes.

**Why.** The aim is not another chat app. It is a way to reach people who would never answer a stranger: a proposal is judged on its
merit by the other side's agent before anyone spends their time. A server-based messenger depends on its company; a blockchain
messenger spreads conversations across the network. Neither fits a network with no centre and no shared copy of private talk.

**Documents:** 21 (new), README.

## 12. The fee pays witnesses

*Agreed later on 13 October, after a review of the questions regulators ask. Revises entries 6 and 7.*

**Before.** The 5% fee was divided equally among all super-nodes except the one the deal passed through; during the warm-up it
accumulated in the contract for later (entries 6 and 7).

**Now.**
- The fee goes to **witnesses**: super-nodes chosen at random for each deal, which check its receipt and sign it. The super-node that
  served the deal is not a witness to it.
- Its size is a **constant in code, set by modelling and never above 5%**. Until the modelling is done, it is 5%.
- The warm-up changes nothing: from the first deal, the fee goes to that deal's witnesses. Nothing accumulates in the contract.

**Why.** An equal share of every deal paid every super-node from other people's work, whether or not it did anything for that deal —
income from the efforts of others, which is exactly what regulators look for. A pot accumulated during the warm-up would be paid out at
the start to whoever then holds super-nodes, so whoever pushed the network to its start could get the cost back. A witness is paid for
work it actually does on that deal, and it is chosen at random, so nobody chooses who checks their own deals. The ceiling of 5% keeps
the fee where entry 7 put it; modelling may lower it to what checking a receipt really costs.

**Documents:** 00, 04, 05, 06, 09, 17, README.

## 13. The founder and related persons run no super-nodes

*Revises entry 9.*

**Before.** The founder could run super-nodes, named them publicly and entered without the deposit-free privilege (entry 9).

**Now.**
- The founder and persons related to them, **Fractera, Inc. included**, run no super-nodes and act as no witness.
- They name their addresses publicly in advance, and the contracts refuse those addresses the role of super-node and of witness.
- The founder's 1% with its twelve-month lock stays; it is their only share.

**Why.** Super-nodes now receive the witness fee and most of the issuance (entry 14). A founder who ran super-nodes would earn from the
network they designed on top of their 1% — the clearest possible advantage, and the one a regulator asks about first. A contract sees
addresses, not people, so it can bind only the addresses that are named; the public statement binds the person.

**Documents:** 00, 05, 06, 15, README.

## 14. Issuance shares: no share for customer agents

*Revises entry 2.*

**Before.** Each period's reward went 1% to the founder, then 50% to super-nodes, 30% to provider agents and 20% to customer agents,
each by the weight of their receipts (entry 2) — that is 49.5%, 29.7% and 19.8% of the whole.

**Now.**
- **49.5%** to super-nodes, by the weight of the receipts they served.
- **29.7%** to provider agents, by the weight of the receipts of their paid work.
- **19.8%** in equal parts to the super-nodes that passed the quality minimum in that period (entry 16).
- **1%** to the founder, with its twelve-month lock.
- Customer agents receive no coins.

**Why.** A customer who receives coins for paying for a service is, in effect, buying coins with that payment — which makes the network
look like a seller of coins to the public. It also rewards a customer for ordering work from itself. A provider earns coins for work it
did; a super-node earns them for deals it served and, in equal parts, for staying available and good enough. Equal parts cannot be
enlarged with fake volume.

**Documents:** 00, 05, README.

## 15. Entry of super-nodes: free, by invitation, then by overload

*Revises entry 10 and answers its open question on entry beyond the first 100.*

**Before.** The first 100 joined without a deposit; entry beyond them was open — a threshold of brought participants, perhaps an
auction for places (entry 10, open questions).

**Now.**
- **Places 1–100**: without a deposit, as in entry 10; the deposit is built from the operator's own rewards.
- **Places 101–1,000** open regardless of the network's load, by **invitation only to owners of provider agents with paid work over the
  last year**. One ticket per address. The deposit is small, the same for everyone, and paid in coins the applicant earned.
- An applicant's server is **measured by random agents, not by super-nodes**. Places are assigned **by random selection** among applicants whose servers
  passed, with diversity of networks and regions so that one applicant with many servers cannot take many places.
- **After 1,000**, new places open only when the network is overloaded — when deals per super-node exceed a constant — **two places at a
  time**, by the same random selection.
- The rule "bring participants" and the auction for places are removed.
- The numbers — the deposit, the overload constant — are set by modelling.

**Why.** At the start nobody has coins, so a deposit in coins cannot be paid. Tying later entry to a year of paid work as a provider lets
in people the network already knows by their work, not by their money, and a deposit in earned coins sells nothing to anyone. Existing
super-nodes gain from having fewer competitors, so they must not be the ones who measure newcomers. Random selection among those who passed
replaces ranking by power or by the number of operations, which would start a race for hardware and reward load generated by oneself.

**Documents:** 00, 01, 05, 06, 15, README.

## 16. Rotation and the quality minimum

*New.*

**Before.** A super-node kept its place for as long as it wished.

**Now.**
- Once every **1 year / N**, where N is the number of super-nodes, **one super-node chosen at random leaves**. There is no penalty: its
  deposit is returned. Its place is assigned by the random selection of entry 15. On average, a super-node stays about a year.
- When the network is overloaded, two more places open by the same random selection (entry 15).
- Every period, random agents check each super-node against a **quality minimum: passed or failed**. A super-node that fails for several
  periods leaves.

**Why.** A permanent place is a stock that never melts — the problem entry 3 solved for search: whoever entered early would keep the
place for ever. Rotation keeps the door open to people who do paid work now. Leaving by rotation is not a fault, so it costs nothing.
The minimum is a single pass or fail rather than a score, so there is nothing to race for.

**Documents:** 05, 06, 15, README.

## 17. Words: a node is a server

*New.*

**Before.** The glossary called a node "a person's own space for agents: an ordinary computer".

**Now.** A **node** is a server that runs agents and serves them to the network. Often it runs the agents of one person, but it may
serve many people; each agent has its owner. A node is not a super-node. The two sides of a deal are the **customer agent** and the
**provider agent**.

**Why.** Services that run agents for many people are nodes too; calling a node "a person's computer" described only one case.

**Documents:** README.

## Contradictions resolved

- **Downtime is not penalised** (document 06). Document 16 described downtime as leading to `slashValidator()` and "Jail"; it now
  follows 06.
- **The network does not depend on our domain.** `paymaster.lagrix.dev` (documents 12, 13) and `get.lagrix.dev` (document 15) are
  removed: the paymaster is a contract address, and the operator's tools come from the repository's releases.
- **Discovery runs through Nostr and the super-node's index** (document 17). Documents 12 and 13 described a separate Kademlia service
  registry; they now follow 17. The SDK remembers a provider it has found and does not search again for every task.
- **A vacancy reopens on the terms of the day it reopens** (entries 10, 15, 16). Documents 05 and 06 said that a vacated place
  reopens on the terms on which it was taken; they now follow this changelog.

## Open questions

These are not decided in this revision and are marked where they appear. The entry of super-nodes beyond the first 100 and the
live-agent check, open in the first part of this revision, are answered by entries 15 and 16.

- **The source of randomness.** Witnesses, the selection of places and rotation all need a random choice that no participant can
  predict or steer. The source is not chosen.
- **How "passed or failed" is measured.** Entry 16 says random agents check each super-node against a quality minimum; what they
  measure, how agents are chosen and how their results are combined is not decided.
- **The number of witnesses per deal**, and what happens while the network has too few super-nodes to choose them from.
- **The `superNode` field of a deal.** The customer names the super-node that receives a deal's receipt (document 04); nothing yet ties
  it to the node that actually served the deal.
- **Payment for relaying traffic.** Earlier documents disagreed — in $LGX, in USDC per megabyte, or none at all. Until it is decided,
  relaying is described without a price.

en.title: 1. Network Topology: Kademlia DHT, Node ID and Routing Algorithms
en.text:
# 1. Network Topology: Kademlia DHT, Node ID and Routing Algorithms

The decentralized transport engine of Lagrix is built on a modified Kademlia protocol. The standard Kademlia implementation is vulnerable to Sybil attacks, so our architecture rigidly binds P2P identifiers to Web3 staking. This creates a financial barrier to entering the routing table.

## 1.1 Node ID Generation and Crypto-Economic Binding

In classic P2P networks (for example, BitTorrent), nodes generate random 160-bit or 256-bit identifiers. In Lagrix this is strictly forbidden.

The Super-Node identifier (NodeID) is deterministically computed from the public key of the wallet (Ethereum/EVM-compatible) from which the guarantee deposit was made into the ValidatorStaking.sol smart contract.

Formula: $NodeID = \text{SHA3-256}(PublicKey_{EVM})$

Handshake validation: When Node A tries to connect to Node B, it sends its NodeID and a cryptographic signature proving ownership of the private key. Node B takes the public key, queries a blockchain RPC node and checks that this address is an active super-node — it has entered under document 05, section 5.6 (a place assigned at random and a deposit in earned coins, or, for places 1-100, a deposit being built from their own rewards) and is not excluded (document 06): `isActiveValidator(PublicKey) == true`.

Result: If the address is not an active super-node, the connection is dropped instantly at the socket level. An attacker cannot fill the network with a million fake NodeIDs, because each one requires a real entry: participants checked for a month and a deposit at stake.

## 1.2 Routing Mathematics (XOR Metric)

Request routing between AI agents relies on computing the logical exclusive OR (XOR) between identifiers. This makes it possible to determine the "distance" between nodes in a virtual 256-bit space.

Distance: $d(x, y) = x \oplus y$

Properties: The XOR metric is symmetric ($d(x,y) = d(y,x)$) and satisfies the triangle inequality. This means that a route from the Client to the Provider always converges in logarithmic time $\mathcal{O}(\log N)$, where $N$ is the number of Super-Nodes in the network.

In practice: If an agent needs to find a Node with ID 0xABCD..., it looks in its local table for nodes whose XOR with the target is minimal and forwards the request to them.

## 1.3 Routing Tables (K-Buckets)

Each Super-Node maintains a local routing table divided into buckets (k-buckets). In a 256-bit space there are 256 buckets.

Parameter $k$: Each bucket stores at most $k=20$ active nodes. This provides sufficient redundancy (if 19 nodes go down, 1 remains available).

Eviction policy: Kademlia gives preference to "old" nodes. If a bucket is full, the new node is placed in a waiting buffer. A PING is sent to the existing nodes. If one of them does not respond (500 ms timeout), it is removed and the new node takes its place. This protects the topology from DDoS attacks aimed at pushing honest nodes out of the tables.

## 1.4 P2P Message Lifecycle (RPC Methods)

Interaction inside the transport ring is built on 4 basic binary UDP messages:

| RPC Method | Purpose in the Lagrix architecture |
|---|---|
| PING | Checks that a node is alive. Used to keep k-buckets up to date. |
| STORE | Writes metadata. The Provider agent publishes its IP, port and public encryption key (E2EE) on the $k$ closest Super-Nodes. |
| FIND_NODE | Requests a list of $k$ nodes closest to the target ID. Used to build the network map. |
| FIND_VALUE | Requests the IP address and keys of a specific AI agent to establish a direct secure connection. |

## 1.5 Integration with the Local Data Plane (Envoy)

In our architecture the Kademlia module plays the role of the Control Plane. It does not move the actual gigabytes of data between AI agents.

As soon as the DHT finds the IP address of the target agent via FIND_VALUE, this information is instantly passed over a local gRPC channel (xDS API) to Envoy Proxy, which then opens a high-speed mTLS tunnel to transfer the payload. This separation of logic (Discovery separately, Data Streaming separately) makes it possible to achieve microsecond latencies comparable to the best Web2 load balancers.

en.title: 2. P2P & NAT Traversal: Breaking Through Firewalls and Relay Bridges
en.text:
# 2. P2P & NAT Traversal: Breaking Through Firewalls and Relay Bridges

Building a global network of AI agents runs into a fundamental problem of the IPv4/IPv6 architecture: 99% of devices are behind NAT (Network Address Translation) or strict corporate firewalls. Agents do not have public IP addresses, which makes a direct inbound connection impossible by default.

In Lagrix v6.0 we implement a custom ICE (Interactive Connectivity Establishment) stack integrated with the protocol's crypto-economics.

## 2.1 Anatomy of the Problem and Node Roles in NAT Traversal

In classic Web2 this problem is solved with centralized STUN/TURN servers from Google or Twilio. In our architecture this role is taken over by decentralized Super-Nodes (Core Relays), which have dedicated "white" (public) IP addresses, because their operators put up a stake and maintain the infrastructure.

NAT types the protocol works with:

Full Cone / Restricted Cone NAT (home networks): Allow UDP Hole Punching.

Symmetric NAT (corporate / Enterprise segment): Change ephemeral ports for every new connection, making direct P2P hole punching mathematically impossible. Require a Relay fallback.

## 2.2 Phase 1: STUN Identification (Endpoint Discovery)

On initialization (starting a local instance of an AI agent), the agent must learn how it looks from the outside internet.

Binding Request: The client agent (Edge Node) sends a STUN_BINDING UDP packet to 3 random Super-Nodes.

Mapping Response: The Super-Node reads the packet's IP header and answers the agent: "I see your traffic from IP 203.0.113.5, port 45123".

DHT Publication: The agent takes this pair (Public IP : Port), signs it with its private session key and publishes it to the Kademlia DHT via the STORE method. Now any Client in the network knows where to knock to find this Provider.

## 2.3 Phase 2: UDP Hole Punching Mechanics (Direct Connection)

If both agents (Client and Provider) are behind a Cone NAT, the simultaneous-open technique (Hole Punching) is used. This is the fastest and free (in terms of gas) way to communicate.

Initiation: Agent A (Client) wants to send a prompt to Agent B (Provider). Agent A asks the DHT for B's public address.

Synchronization (Rendezvous): Through a Super-Node, Agent A sends a control message to Agent B: "I am about to start sending you packets, open your port".

Simultaneous punch:

Agent A sends a UDP packet to B's public address. Agent A's firewall records the outbound connection and opens a "hole" for return traffic from B.

At the same time Agent B sends a UDP packet to A's public address. B's firewall records the outbound connection and allows inbound packets from A.

Result: The packets cross in the providers' routers. A direct, microsecond P2P channel is formed. The Super-Nodes no longer take part in the transfer, saving bandwidth.

## 2.4 Phase 3: Relay Fallback (TURN Bridges for Enterprise)

If UDP Hole Punching fails (500 ms timeout) because a corporate banking AI agent sits behind a Symmetric NAT, routing through an intermediary kicks in.

This is where Lagrix crypto-economics comes into play:

Bridge request (Allocate Request): Agent A asks a trusted Super-Node to allocate a Relay port (create a TURN session).

Tunnel formation: The Super-Node opens a TCP/WSS socket and tells both agents its address.

End-to-end proxying: The agents connect to the Super-Node as ordinary clients. The Super-Node blindly forwards encrypted bytes from A to B and back.

Payment for relaying: whether and how a super-node is paid for the traffic it relays is an open question of the changelog (document 000); until it is decided, relaying is described without a price. A super-node already earns its share of every period's reward for the deals it serves and an equal share of the fee of the deals it does not serve (documents 05, 09).

## 2.5 Connection Establishment State Machine

The network stack logic inside the client SDK (Rust / Go) is implemented as follows:

Gathering all candidates (Local IP, Public STUN IP, Relay IP).

Parallel ping (Connectivity Checks) across all routes at once.

Priority selection (Nomination):

Priority 0: Local network (LAN) — 0 ms.

Priority 1: UDP Hole Punching — 10-50 ms (Free).

Priority 2: TCP Relay Fallback — 50-150 ms (relayed by a super-node).

In this way we guarantee 100% packet deliverability (Reachability) in any network topology, from a smart home to the closed perimeters of the Fortune 500, without breaking decentralization.

en.title: 3. Encryption and Proxying: Envoy Proxy, Web3-mTLS and E2EE Isolation
en.text:
# 3. Encryption and Proxying: Envoy Proxy, Web3-mTLS and E2EE Isolation

Separating discovery logic (the Control Plane, implemented through the Kademlia DHT) from data transfer (the Data Plane) is a classic pattern of high-load systems. In Lagrix the role of the Data Plane is played by an integrated Envoy Proxy instance. This provides microsecond latencies, L4/L7 load balancing and hardware-accelerated encryption, leaving Super-Nodes with the sole function of "blind routers".

## 3.1 Envoy Proxy as the Data Plane (Sidecar Pattern)

Every AI agent (both client and provider) in the Lagrix network is deployed together with a lightweight Envoy sidecar container.

Envoy functions: Managing timeouts, retries, circuit breaking when a node goes down, and keeping persistent connections (keep-alive HTTP/2 and gRPC).

Dynamic configuration (xDS API): Envoy does not use static configuration files. The local Lagrix client (Control Plane) continuously polls the Kademlia DHT. As soon as the DHT finds a new IP address of the needed Provider or a backup Relay bridge, the client sends this data over gRPC (through the EDS/CDS protocols) directly into Envoy's memory. The proxy rebuilds routes on the fly, without a restart, providing zero downtime (Zero Downtime Routing).

## 3.2 Web3-Native mTLS (Mutual Authentication)

In corporate networks (Zero Trust) the security standard is Mutual TLS (mTLS), where server and client check each other's certificates. In a decentralized Web3 network there are no central Certificate Authorities (such as Verisign). Lagrix solves this with elliptic-curve cryptography (secp256k1).

Ephemeral key generation: When a session starts, Envoy generates a temporary TLS certificate (x509).

Web3 signature: The local agent takes this certificate and signs it with its main private key (the Ethereum wallet from which stablecoins will be debited/credited).

Cryptographic handshake:

Agent A connects to Agent B.

They exchange certificates and Web3 signatures.

Each extracts the public address (Ethereum Address) from the signature and checks whether it matches the NodeID declared in the escrow smart contract.

Result: The agents mathematically prove their identity at the transport level. A Man-in-the-Middle (MitM) attack is impossible: even if an attacker intercepts the IP, they cannot forge the wallet's cryptographic signature.

## 3.3 E2EE and Payload Isolation (Payload Blindness)

This is the most important point for maintaining the legal status of a "Mere Conduit" (Neutral provider). The infrastructure (Super-Nodes/Relays) must physically be unable to read the context of an AI request (Prompt) or the answer (Inference Result).

A multi-layer envelope architecture (Onion-lite routing) is used:

Outer layer (Transport): Envoy encapsulates packets in a standard TLS 1.3 tunnel to the Super-Node. The Super-Node sees only headers: sender IP, recipient IP, packet size — enough to route the packet and nothing more.

Inner layer (Payload E2EE): The data itself (for example, JSON with a system prompt) is encrypted with a symmetric key (AES-256-GCM or ChaCha20-Poly1305). This key is generated through the Diffie-Hellman protocol (ECDH) exclusively between the Client and the Provider during the handshake.

Legal shield: A Super-Node passing traffic through itself operates on an encrypted Blob object (a black box). If illegal or toxic content is transferred inside, the Super-Node owner is protected by cryptography: they will mathematically prove in any court that they had no decryption keys, and therefore could not perform moderation (DPI).

## 3.4 Metadata Obfuscation (Protection Against Traffic Analysis)

Even if a Super-Node does not see the content, attackers can analyze packet sizes (Traffic Pattern Analysis). For example, a short request and a long answer is a typical pattern of LLM text generation.
To protect the confidentiality of corporate clients:

Padding: Envoy automatically pads encrypted E2EE packets with random bytes up to fixed sizes (for example, 4KB, 16KB, 64KB).

Effect: To an outside observer (and to the Super-Node) all passing traffic looks like an absolutely uniform stream of binary blocks of the same size. Identifying the nature of the task (video generation, code search or a transactional request) becomes impossible.

en.title: 4. The Escrow Smart Contract: A2AEscrow.sol (EIP-712, Time-Lock, Fee and Receipts)
en.text:
# 4. The Escrow Smart Contract: A2AEscrow.sol (EIP-712, Time-Lock, Fee and Receipts)
