The A2AEscrow.sol smart contract is the financial core of Lagrix. Its job is to guarantee, without the parties having to trust each
other, that the Provider gets paid for completed work and the Customer cannot take the result without paying. Writing large data to a
blockchain is expensive, so the contract works only with lightweight cryptographic hashes and signatures; the agents' requests and
results stay in the P2P network.

A closed deal in this contract is the source of everything else in the network: the fee is taken from it (document 09), a receipt
for the super-node is born from it (document 05), and the participants' history is updated.

## 4.1 The deal life cycle

The escrow logic is a strict finite state machine.

```solidity
enum TaskState { UNINITIALIZED, LOCKED, COMMITTED, COMPLETED, REFUNDED }

struct Task {
    uint96 amount;        // payment in USDC (up to $79 billion, 96 bits are enough)
    uint40 lockedAt;      // when the funds were locked
    uint40 commitTime;    // when the Provider submitted the result
    TaskState state;      // current state
    address customer;     // the Customer
    address provider;     // the Provider — the only one who may perform the task
    address superNode;    // the super-node the deal passed through; it gets the receipt
}
```

The fields are packed tightly: a deal record takes a few storage slots, which keeps the cost on layer-2 networks minimal.

- **LOCKED.** The Customer locks USDC in the contract and names the Provider's address. Nobody else can take over the order.
- **COMMITTED.** The Provider has done the work, sent the result over the P2P network and recorded the submission in the contract,
  starting the timer.
- **COMPLETED.** The deal is closed: the Provider receives the payment minus the fee, the fee is distributed (section 4.4), and the
  super-node gets a receipt (section 4.5).
- **REFUNDED.** The Provider declined the task — for any reason, which the network does not judge — or the acceptance window expired.
  The funds return to the Customer in full, and no fee is taken.

## 4.2 Cryptographic receipts (EIP-712)

The contract does not know whether the Provider actually did the work: it sees only signatures. Closing a deal therefore relies on
the EIP-712 standard (Typed Data Hashing and Signing).

- **Off-chain signature.** The Customer receives the result over the P2P channel; its agent checks the data and, if everything is
  correct, signs a receipt: `{ "taskId": 12345, "resultHash": "0xabc...", "amount": 5000000 }`.
- **On-chain execution.** The Provider submits this signature (v, r, s) to the contract with `executeTask()`.
- **Verification.** The contract recovers the address from the signature (`ecrecover`). If it is the Customer of this deal, the deal
  moves to COMPLETED.

## 4.3 Time-Lock: protecting the Provider from a hang

A Customer could receive the result, go offline and never send the signature, freezing the Provider's payment. The function
`claimTimeout(uint256 taskId)` protects against this.

- **Commitment.** Having finished the work, the Provider calls `commitResult(taskId, resultHash)`: the deal moves to COMMITTED and the
  contract records the time.
- **Dispute window.** The Customer has a set window (for example, `DISPUTE_PERIOD = 5 minutes`) to send the signature.
- **Automatic closing.** When the window has passed, the Provider calls `claimTimeout(taskId)`. The contract checks
  `block.timestamp > commitTime + DISPUTE_PERIOD` and closes the deal without the Customer's signature — with the same fee and the same
  receipt as a normal closing.

## 4.4 Splitting the payment and the fee

When a deal moves to COMPLETED, the contract splits the amount:

| To whom | Share | Where |
|---|---|---|
| The Provider | the rest (95% while the fee is 5%) | to its wallet |
| The network fee | at most 5%, set by modelling | deducted from the deal amount and paid to the deal's witnesses under document 09 |

The fee goes to witnesses: super-nodes chosen at random for the deal, which check its receipt and sign it; the super-node the deal
passed through is never one of them (document 09). It is taken from the very
first deal, including the warm-up before issuance starts (document 05, section 5.2).

## 4.5 The receipt and the participants' history

A closed deal emits an event from which receipts and history are built:

```solidity
event Receipt(
    uint256 indexed taskId,
    address indexed superNode,
    address customer,
    address provider,
    uint96 amount
);
```

- **The receipt.** A `Receipt` event counts for the customer, the provider and the super-node `superNode`, each with a weight equal to
  the deal amount. Receipts divide each issuance period's reward (document 05, section 5.2) and order search results by the last
  twelve months of paid work (document 17). Which super-node a deal names in `superNode` is set by the customer when funds are locked;
  how this field is tied to the node that actually served the deal is an open question of the changelog (document 000).
- **The participants' history.** The contract updates, for both parties, the number of closed deals and the time of the last deal —
  separately as provider and as customer — and records the joining time of a new participant. The six-month rule (document 05) relies on
  this data.

## 4.6 Cost

Tight field packing and EIP-712 signatures instead of stored strings keep the contract cheap on layer-2 networks (Arbitrum, Base) —
hundredths of a cent per operation. This is critical for micro-deals between AI agents.

en.title: 5. $LGX Tokenomics: Coins Are Born From the Network's Work
en.text:
# 5. $LGX Tokenomics: Coins Are Born From the Network's Work

$LGX is the coin of the Lagrix network. No coins are sold at launch: each one is created only when the network does useful work —
agents close paid deals and super-nodes serve them. This document describes how coins appear, who receives them, what they are for,
and which rules protect the network from those who come to trade rather than to work.

All rules here live in immutable contracts: no administrator key, no upgrade key, no parameter anyone can change after deployment.
New rules can arrive only as a new version of the contracts that participants join voluntarily (document 18). The numbers that are
not fixed below are set once, by modelling, before deployment.

## 5.1 Key properties

| Property | Value |
|---|---|
| Issuance cap | 1,000,000,000 LGX over about 30 years |
| How coins appear | only as the reward of an issuance period, divided by the receipts of that period (section 5.2) |
| Sale at launch | none: no presale, no investor allocation, no fund created in advance |
| Issuance schedule | declines smoothly, so issuance fades rather than stopping on a cliff; the exact shape is set by modelling |
| Start of issuance | after the warm-up: a threshold of paid deal volume and a minimum number of super-nodes (section 5.2) |
| Deal fee | a constant of at most 5% of the deal amount, set by modelling (5% until then), paid to witnesses (section 5.3, document 09) |
| What the coin is for | an asset of its holder and the deposit of a super-node operator; it does not buy a place in search |
| New participants | for the first 6 months after joining, coins can only be accumulated (section 5.4) |
| Founder's share | 1% of every period's reward; each portion can be sold no earlier than 12 months after its period (section 5.5) |

## 5.2 Receipts and issuance by period

Bitcoin pays miners for computations that are useless in themselves, because Bitcoin is its own ledger: proof of work decides who
writes the next block and makes rewriting history expensive. Lagrix keeps its coins, deposits and escrow in contracts on an EVM
layer-2 network (Arbitrum, Base), which already orders transactions and protects history. Lagrix therefore needs no mining: it pays
for what the network exists for — deals between agents that it has served.

**Receipt.** When a deal between a customer and a provider is closed in escrow (document 04), the contract records a receipt — a record
of a completed, paid deal for the customer, the provider and the super-node it passed through. A receipt's weight is the deal amount in
USDC, not the number of messages: a thousand messages inside one deal give one receipt.

**Issuance period.** A block of Lagrix is a period set by the contract, not something found. At the end of every period the contract
issues that period's reward from the schedule and divides it by the weight of the receipts closed in the period. Nobody can find,
forge or add a period, and a receipt cannot be forged: it is the closing of a paid deal.

**Splitting the reward.**

| Who | Share of the reward | How it is distributed |
|---|---|---|
| The founder | 1% | into the 12-month rolling lock (section 5.5) |
| Super-nodes, by work | 49.5% | in proportion to the weight of the receipts of the deals they served in this period |
| Provider agents | 29.7% | in proportion to the weight of the receipts of their paid work in this period |
| Super-nodes, equally | 19.8% | in equal parts to the super-nodes that passed the quality minimum in this period (section 5.6) |
| **Total** | **100%** | |

Coins go to those who do the work and those who serve it. Customer agents receive no coins: a customer who received coins for paying for
a service would in effect be buying coins with that payment.

**The warm-up start.** The network begins working on real deals with real money before any coin exists, like an engine that turns over
on the starter before it fires:

- the fee is taken from the very first deal and paid to that deal's witnesses, as always (section 5.3); nothing accumulates in the
  contract;
- no reward is issued until the network has passed a threshold of paid deal volume in USDC and has a minimum number of super-nodes —
  both constants in code, their values set by modelling;
- the first period then opens by itself; nobody presses a button;
- receipts closed during the warm-up earn no coins afterwards.

Taking the fee from the first deal makes the threshold expensive to fake: pushing the network to its start with empty deals would cost
the fee on every one of them, paid to witnesses chosen at random. Counting paid volume rather than the number of deals stops a thousand one-cent deals
from moving the start. Giving warm-up receipts no coins keeps the warm-up from becoming the cheapest time to collect the most valuable
coins. Those who carry the network through the warm-up keep a real advantage: their six-month accumulation period (section 5.4) runs
during it.

## 5.3 The deal fee

The network takes a fee on every deal, in USDC. Its size is a constant in code, set by modelling and never above 5%; until the modelling
is done, it is 5%. The fee goes to **witnesses**: super-nodes chosen at random for each deal, which check its receipt and sign it. The
super-node that served the deal is not a witness to it. The fee is how fake deals are made to cost real money: a deal with oneself, made
to collect receipts, costs the fee on its amount, and the payer does not choose who receives it. The full rules are in document 09.

## 5.4 The six-month rule

For the first six months after joining the network, every participant can only accumulate coins: they cannot be sold or transferred.
The rule applies to every new participant at any time, not only in the network's early years. Buying coins is allowed.

```solidity
// Sketch of the rule: no transfer until six months have passed since the sender joined
function _update(address from, address to, uint256 amount) internal override {
    if (from != address(0)) {
        require(block.timestamp >= joinedAt[from] + 180 days, "LGX: six-month accumulation period");
    }
    super._update(from, to, amount);
}
```

Whoever comes to buy and quickly sell will sell nothing in six months. Whoever comes to work keeps working while the period runs.

## 5.5 The founder

The founder receives 1% of every period's reward for creating the architecture. The share is created together with the period and
grows only while the network actually works; not a single coin is created in advance.

Each portion can be sold no earlier than 12 months after its period. The lock is rolling: the founder never holds a large amount that
could be dumped on the market at once. The share has no administrator keys: it cannot be accelerated, increased or taken away.

```solidity
// Sketch: the founder's portion from period n becomes available 12 months after that period
struct FounderTranche { uint96 amount; uint40 issuedAt; }
function releasable(FounderTranche memory t) public view returns (uint96) {
    return block.timestamp >= t.issuedAt + 365 days ? t.amount : 0;
}
```

**No other advantage.** The founder has no advantage over any participant except this share. The code makes the rest impossible: there
is no pre-mine and no key that issues coins; no key that changes any rule; the start of issuance is triggered by volume, not by a
person; and pushing the start with fake deals costs the fee, which goes to witnesses chosen at random.

**No super-nodes.** The founder and persons related to them, Fractera, Inc. included, run no super-nodes and act as no witness. They
name their addresses publicly in advance, and the contracts refuse those addresses the role of super-node and of witness; everything
these addresses receive is locked for 12 months. Super-nodes receive the witness fee and most of the issuance, so a founder running them
would earn from the network on top of the 1%. A contract sees addresses, not people, so it can bind only the addresses that are named;
the public statement binds the person.

## 5.6 How new super-nodes join

A super-node is a permanent server that keeps the discovery index, builds search results, helps agents connect and checks and signs the receipts of deals; payment itself is settled by the escrow contract (document 04)
(documents 01, 02, 06, 17). Places open in three stages, and every place is assigned at random, not bought:

- **Places 1–100: without a deposit.** At the start no coins exist, so a deposit cannot be paid. Instead, an operator's first rewards
  stay locked as their deposit until it reaches the required size, and penalties are taken from it (document 06). The privilege belongs
  to the operator, not to the place.
- **Places 101–1,000: by invitation.** These places open regardless of the network's load. Invitations go only to owners of provider
  agents with paid work over the last year; one ticket per address. The deposit is small, the same for everyone, and paid in coins the
  applicant earned — it sells nothing to anyone.
- **After 1,000: by overload.** New places open only when the network is overloaded — when deals per super-node exceed a constant — two
  places at a time.
- **Measurement by random agents.** An applicant's server is measured by agents chosen at random, not by super-nodes: existing
  super-nodes gain from having fewer competitors, so they must not be the ones who judge newcomers.
- **Random selection with diversity.** Places are assigned at random among applicants whose servers passed, with diversity of networks and regions, so
  that one applicant with many servers cannot take many places. Ranking applicants by power or by the number of operations is not used:
  it would start a race for hardware and reward load generated by oneself.
- **Rotation.** Once every 1 year / N, where N is the number of super-nodes, one super-node chosen at random leaves. There is no
  penalty: its deposit is returned. Its place is assigned by the same random selection, on the terms of the day it reopens. On average a super-node stays
  about a year, so the door stays open to those who do paid work now.
- **The quality minimum.** Every period, random agents check each super-node against a minimum: passed or failed. Those who passed
  share 19.8% of the period's reward equally (section 5.2); a super-node that fails for several periods leaves.
- **Vacancies.** A place freed by rotation, by failing the minimum or by removal for fraud (document 06) reopens on the terms of the day
  it reopens, never on the terms of the operator who left.

The numbers — the deposit, the overload constant, how many failed periods lead to leaving — are set by modelling. The source of
randomness for the selection of places and rotation, and how "passed or failed" is measured, are open questions (document 000).

## 5.7 What $LGX does not have

- No sale of coins at launch and no allocation for investors.
- No fund created in advance and no keys that let anyone create coins outside the issuance schedule.
- No mechanism whose only purpose is price.
- No place in search: ranking follows paid work, not coins (document 17).
- Lagrix makes no promise about the price of $LGX. It is an asset of its holder and the deposit of a super-node operator.

## 5.8 Why $LGX issuance is tied to the network's work

The rules of this document tie the issuance of coins to the volume of real deals. The link comes from the rules themselves, not from
promises.

**The link through the fee.** New coins go to receipts, and every receipt is a deal from which a fee in USDC was deducted and paid to
witnesses (document 09). If the value of the coins issued per dollar of deals rises above the fee rate, it becomes profitable to make
deals only for the receipts: pay the fee and get more back in coins. Such receipts multiply, and each receipt earns fewer coins — until
the profit disappears. So the value of the new coins the network issues in a period tends toward the fee's share of the deal volume in
that period:

```
value_of_coins_issued_in_period ≈ fee_rate × deal_volume_in_period
```

**What this link does not do.**
- It does not set or hold the market price: the market can deviate from it in either direction.
- An upward deviation is corrected slowly: coins earned by new participants cannot be sold for the first six months.
- A downward deviation corrects nothing except that serving deals for coins becomes less profitable.
- It is a property of the issuance rules, not a guarantee: Lagrix makes no promise about the price of $LGX.

The exact equilibrium values are set by modelling the network.

en.title: 6. Super-node Deposits: Downtime and Fraud
en.text:
# 6. Super-node Deposits: Downtime and Fraud

Super-nodes are the backbone of Lagrix: they keep the discovery table, build search results, help agents connect and check and sign
the receipts of deals; payment itself is settled by the escrow contract (document 04). The ValidatorStaking.sol contract ties a server's behaviour in the network to its operator's deposit. The main rule of
this document: **downtime is not fraud**. A server that goes offline simply stops earning; coins are taken only for proven fraud.

## 6.1 The deposit

The deposit is set by the place the operator receives (document 05, section 5.6). Operators of places 1–100 join without a deposit:
their first rewards stay locked as the deposit until it reaches the required size, and penalties are taken from what has accumulated.
Later operators lock a small deposit, the same for everyone, in coins they earned.
On withdrawal the deposit stays locked for 14 days: if fraud committed before the withdrawal comes to light in that time, the penalty
can still be collected.

```solidity
struct Validator {
    uint96 stakeBalance;    // locked deposit in LGX
    uint40 lastSeen;        // last confirmed availability
    uint40 unbondingFrom;   // start of the 14-day withdrawal (0 if none)
    uint16 slashCount;      // number of proven violations
    bool   blacklisted;     // permanently excluded for forgery
    address pubKeyAddress;  // address bound to the NodeID
}
```

## 6.2 Downtime is not fraud

As in Bitcoin, where a miner that is switched off simply finds no blocks, a super-node is not penalised for downtime.

- **While the node is unavailable,** it serves no deals, so it earns no receipts and no share of the period's reward; it is not chosen
  as a witness, so it receives no fee; and it does not pass the period's quality minimum. It loses only income.
- **Availability** is measured by neighbouring nodes: regular checks (PING) from the Kademlia table (document 01).
- **If the node is unavailable for 30 days in a row, or fails the quality minimum for several periods,** it is removed. Its place
  reopens on the terms of the day it reopens (document 05, section 5.6), and the deposit is returned to the operator after the 14-day
  withdrawal. It did not cheat — it left.
- **Rotation is not a penalty either.** Once every 1 year / N a super-node chosen at random leaves; its deposit is returned in the same
  way (document 05, section 5.6).

## 6.3 Fraud and its proof

A blockchain cannot see IP packets, so fraud is proven by receipts and checks that anyone can repeat.

**Packet dropping.** A customer (agent A) sends traffic to a provider (agent B) through super-node R. Agent A signs the packet;
agent B signs a receipt of delivery. If R accepted the packet for relaying but B's receipt is missing, agent A sends a
`TRACE_REQUEST`; three independent neighbours confirm that R accepted the packet and did not pass it on — this forms a Fraud Proof.

**Falsified results.** The random places in search results are calculated verifiably (document 17, section 17.3). A result list in
which a random place does not match the calculation is a ready proof: the contract checks the super-node's signature on it and the
calculation data.

**Forged tables and NodeID hijacking.** An attempt to forge Kademlia DHT records or to impersonate another node is proven by
signatures that do not match the node's key.

## 6.4 Penalties

| Violation | Proof | Penalty |
|---|---|---|
| Downtime | unavailability to neighbours | **none**; the node loses income and after 30 days is removed with its deposit returned |
| Packet dropping | Fraud Proof with a missing receipt | 10% of the deposit |
| Falsified results | results that do not match the verifiable calculation | 25% of the deposit |
| Forged tables, NodeID hijacking | signatures that do not match | 100% of the deposit and permanent exclusion |

**Where the taken coins go.** Half goes to whoever proved the violation: a reward for keeping the network honest. The other half is
removed from circulation for good — as in Bitcoin, where an unclaimed reward is simply lost. No new coins are issued to replace it, so
the final number of coins ends up below 1,000,000,000 by exactly that amount.

```
[Customer agent] --(packet)--> [Super-node R] --X (dropped)--> [Provider agent]
       |                                                              |
       +---------------- (TRACE_REQUEST, waiting for receipt) --------+
                                      |
                              [Fraud Proof]
                                      |
                                      v
                       [ValidatorStaking.sol: slashValidator()]
                                      |
                    +-----------------+-----------------+
                    |                                   |
          (50% to whoever proved it)        (50% removed from circulation)
```

## 6.5 Protection against false reports

So that the contract is not flooded with fake proofs, calling `slashValidator()` requires the reporter to lock a small deposit.

- **The proof is valid:** the reporter gets the deposit back and receives half of the penalty.
- **The proof is false:** the reporter's deposit is removed from circulation.

Honest work pays better than risking the deposit, and a false report costs more than silence.

en.title: 7. Smart Contract Testing and Audit: Foundry, Slither and Fuzzing
en.text:
# 7. Smart Contract Testing and Audit: Foundry, Slither and Fuzzing

Lagrix smart contracts handle real money (USDC) and $LGX coins. A bug in a contract is dangerous: the contracts are immutable, with no
administrator or upgrade key (document 18), so a deployed contract cannot be fixed at all — a bug is closed only by a new version that
participants move to. Every contract therefore passes three layers of checks before deployment: Foundry tests, invariant fuzzing and
Slither static analysis.

| Contract | What it does | Document |
|---|---|---|
| A2AEscrow.sol | deals, receipts, Time-Lock, fee deduction, the `Receipt` event | 04 |
| FeeDistributor.sol | the fee shared equally among the super-nodes except the serving one; the reserve before a second node exists | 09 |
| PeriodIssuance.sol | the warm-up threshold, issuance by period on the schedule, the reward split by receipts | 05 |
| SearchVouchers.sol | prepaid balances and batch redemption of search vouchers at the fixed price | 17 |
| LagrixToken.sol | the coin, the supply cap, the six-month rule, the founder's tranches | 05 |
| ValidatorStaking.sol | deposits, removal, penalties, false reports | 06 |
| FeedbackRegistry.sol | likes and dislikes bound to deal receipts | 17 |

## 7.1 Unit and integration tests (Foundry)

Foundry tests are written in Solidity itself and run at the speed of compiled code. Key scenarios:

- `test_A2AEscrow_StateTransitions()` — LOCKED → COMMITTED → COMPLETED transitions and rejection of invalid calls (for example,
  `claimTimeout()` before the dispute window expires).
- `test_EIP712_SignatureReplay()` — a signature cannot be reused with another `taskId` or nonce.
- `test_FeeSplit_95_5()` — on closing, the provider gets exactly 95% and the fee exactly 5%; a refund takes no fee.
- `test_Fee_SharedExceptServingNode()` — the fee of a deal is credited in equal shares to every active super-node except the one that served it; with no other node it goes to the reserve.
- `test_WarmUp_NoIssuanceBeforeThreshold()` — no reward is issued before the paid-volume threshold and the minimum number of super-nodes; warm-up receipts earn nothing afterwards.
- `test_SearchVoucher_ExactPrice()` — a voucher for any amount other than the fixed price is rejected, and a used nonce cannot be redeemed again.
- `test_SixMonthRule()` — a coin transfer earlier than 180 days after joining is rejected; after that it passes.
- `test_FounderTranche_12Months()` — a founder's tranche from a block is unavailable before 12 months and available after (`vm.warp()`).
- `test_PeriodReward_Split()` — 1% to the founder, then 50/30/20 of the rest by receipt weight, accurate to 1 wei.
- `test_NoAdminFunctions()` — no function changes a rate, a price, a threshold or the schedule after deployment.
- `test_Downtime_NoSlash()` — an unavailable node is not penalised and after 30 days is removed with its deposit returned.
- `test_Slashing_HalfToReporter_HalfRemoved()` — half of a penalty to the reporter, half removed from circulation.

```solidity
// Example: Time-Lock in A2AEscrow.t.sol
function test_CannotClaimTimeoutBeforeDisputePeriod() public {
    vm.prank(customer);
    escrow.lockFunds(taskId, provider, superNode, 100 * 10**6); // lock 100 USDC (6 decimals)

    vm.prank(provider);
    escrow.commitResult(taskId, resultHash);

    // try to collect after 2 minutes, before the 5-minute window expires
    vm.warp(block.timestamp + 2 minutes);

    vm.prank(provider);
    vm.expectRevert(A2AEscrow.DisputePeriodNotExpired.selector);
    escrow.claimTimeout(taskId);
}
```

## 7.2 Fuzzing and invariants

Unit tests check the scenarios the developer thought of. Fuzzing feeds millions of random inputs — edge values, zero addresses, huge
amounts — and checks invariants that must hold for any sequence of calls:

1. **Escrow solvency.** The escrow contract's USDC balance is never below the sum of all locked deals.
2. **Fee solvency.** FeeDistributor's USDC balance is never below the sum of all credited but unclaimed fee shares plus the reserve.
3. **Supply cap.** No more than 1,000,000,000 LGX are ever created.
4. **Founder's tranches.** The founder cannot withdraw more than the tranches that are at least 12 months old.
5. **Deposit accounting.** The sum of all super-nodes' deposits equals the total recorded in the staking contract.

```solidity
function invariant_EscrowSolvency() public view {
    assertGe(usdc.balanceOf(address(escrow)), escrow.totalLockedFunds(), "Escrow is insolvent");
}

function invariant_SupplyCap() public view {
    assertLe(token.totalMinted(), 1_000_000_000 * 10**18, "Supply cap exceeded");
}
```

## 7.3 Static analysis (Slither)

Slither translates the code into an intermediate representation and looks for common vulnerabilities:

- **Reentrancy:** protection — the checks → effects → interactions order and OpenZeppelin's `ReentrancyGuard`.
- **Authorization via `tx.origin`:** forbidden; Slither warns about any use of it.
- **Unchecked low-level calls:** token transfers only through `SafeERC20`.
- **Overflows:** built-in checks of Solidity 0.8+ and strict types (`uint96`, `uint40`) for packed fields.

## 7.4 The check pipeline

Every change to the main branch of the open repository goes through the same chain:

```
[ push / pull request ]
       │
       ├──> 1. forge fmt --check               (formatting)
       ├──> 2. slither . --fail-on high|medium  (static analysis)
       ├──> 3. forge test --gas-report          (tests and gas usage)
       └──> 4. forge test --fuzz-runs 10000     (invariant fuzzing)
```

If even one of 10,000 random calls breaks an invariant, the change is not accepted.

en.title: 8. Account Abstraction (ERC-4337): The UserOperation Structure and Bundler Infrastructure
en.text:
# 8. Account Abstraction (ERC-4337): The UserOperation Structure and Bundler Infrastructure

Autonomous AI agents should not manage native blockchain wallets (EOA), having to calculate gas by hand, watch their ETH/MATIC balance and sign raw base transactions. In Lagrix v6.0 we implement an Account Abstraction stack based on the ERC-4337 standard, which turns every AI agent wallet into a programmable smart account (Smart Contract Wallet).

This fully isolates the agent's application logic from blockchain mechanics: the agent operates on a "request-payment" abstraction in USDC, and all the work with network fees is taken over by special aggregator nodes (Bundlers) and the Paymaster contract.

## 8.1 Anatomy of the UserOperation Structure

Instead of standard Ethereum transactions, AI agents form pseudo-transactions — UserOperation (UserOp) objects. The structure packs the agent's intent and is passed over the P2P network of Bundler nodes outside the blockchain's main mempool.

```solidity
struct UserOperation {
    address sender;             // Address of the AI agent's smart account
    uint256 nonce;              // Unique sequential number (Anti-Replay)
    bytes initCode;             // Smart account creation code (if launched for the first time)
    bytes callData;             // Encoded function call (for example, lockFunds in A2AEscrow)
    uint256 callGasLimit;       // Gas limit for executing the application logic
    uint256 verificationGasLimit; // Gas limit for checking signatures and the Paymaster
    uint256 preVerificationGas; // Gas limit to compensate the Bundler's overhead
    uint256 maxFeePerGas;       // Maximum gas price (EIP-1559)
    uint256 maxPriorityFeePerGas;// Tip to the blockchain miner/validator
    bytes paymasterAndData;     // Paymaster contract address + sponsorship signature/conditions
    bytes signature;            // The AI agent's cryptographic signature (secp256k1 / BLS / Passkey)
}
```

Key fields for M2M interaction:

initCode (Lazy Account Deployment): An AI agent is created instantly without transactions on the blockchain. Its smart account is generated off-chain deterministically through CREATE2. The first transaction automatically deploys the account contract thanks to the initCode field.

paymasterAndData: The main integration flag. Contains the address of LagrixPaymaster.sol and parameters indicating that the gas for the transaction is paid not by the agent but by the Paymaster, which deducts the equivalent in USDC.

## 8.2 Bundler Infrastructure: Assembling and Packing Meta-Transactions

A Bundler is a specialized infrastructure node (it can be run by Super-Node operators) that listens to a separate Alt-Mempool for UserOperations.

```
[Client Agent] ---> (UserOp in USDC) ---> [Alt-Mempool (P2P)]
                                                 │
                                                 ▼
                                        [ Bundler Node ]
                                                 │
                             (Packing into a bundle: [UserOp1, UserOp2, ...])
                                                 │
                                                 ▼
                                   [ EntryPoint.sol (On-Chain) ]
                                                 │
                                    ┌────────────┴────────────┐
                                    ▼                         ▼
                          [LagrixPaymaster.sol]       [A2AEscrow.sol]
                         (USDC charged for gas)     (Escrow capture)
```

Step-by-step Bundler algorithm:

Reception and filtering (Validation Phase): The Bundler receives a UserOp through the JSON-RPC method eth_sendUserOperation. It performs an off-chain simulation through the EntryPoint.sol contract, checking:
- The validity of the UserOp.signature.
- That LagrixPaymaster or the agent has a sufficient USDC balance/approval.
- The absence of forbidden opcodes (for example, TIMESTAMP, GASPRICE) that could break execution determinism.

Aggregation (Batching): The Bundler combines 10 to 100 valid UserOps from different AI agents into one standard Ethereum transaction.

Submission to the On-Chain EntryPoint: The Bundler calls the function handleOps(UserOperation[] ops, address beneficiary) on the singleton EntryPoint.sol contract.

Gas compensation: The Bundler pays the native L2 network gas (ETH/Base/Arbitrum) from its own wallet, and the EntryPoint contract instantly compensates its costs from the LagrixPaymaster.sol deposit + accrues a micro-premium (Bundler Fee).

## 8.3 The EntryPoint.sol Contract: The Execution Core

The ERC-4337 standard uses a single EntryPoint contract, proven over the years and deployed at the same addresses in all EVM networks. It acts as a trusted orchestrator.

Lifecycle of a handleOps() call inside EntryPoint:

Verification Loop:
- For each UserOp, the sender account is checked.
- If the account has not been created yet, initCode is executed.
- The validateUserOp() function on the agent's smart account is called to check the ECDSA signature.
- validatePaymasterUserOp() is called on the LagrixPaymaster.sol contract to lock the required amount of USDC to cover gas.

Execution Loop:
- EntryPoint executes the callData of each UserOp (for example, sending a call to A2AEscrow.sol).
- The exact amount of gas actually spent is measured.
- EntryPoint deducts from the Paymaster deposit exactly as much USDC (plus the Bundler premium) as was needed for gas, and returns the unused remainder.

## 8.4 Benefits for the Lagrix Ecosystem

Zero friction (Zero Gas Friction): An AI agent developer only needs to put $10$ USDC on the smart account. The agent will never again need to hold native ETH for transactions.

Session Keys: The agent's smart account makes it possible to limit permissions. A bot can be given a temporary key allowed to spend no more than $1$ USDC per hour and to call exclusively the A2AEscrow.sol contract. If the bot is hacked, the hacker cannot withdraw all the funds from the account.

Atomic Multi-Operations: An agent can do approve(USDC) and lockFunds() in one UserOp, reducing the number of on-chain steps and saving 40% on gas.

en.title: 9. The Deal Fee: Payment to the Witnesses of a Deal
en.text:
# 9. The Deal Fee: Payment to the Witnesses of a Deal

The network takes a fee on every deal. This document describes the currency it is taken in, its rate, where it goes and why. The $LGX
coin plays no part in this mechanism: the fee is money for the work of the network, while $LGX is an asset of its holder and a
super-node's deposit (document 05).

## 9.1 Currency: USDC

Agents pay each other for work in USDC (document 04). The fee is taken in the same currency and paid out in it.

| Why USDC | What it gives |
|---|---|
| The fee costs real money from day one | a fake deal with oneself costs the fee on its amount even while $LGX does not yet exist |
| Payouts make sense to people | "10 cents came in", with no conversion at a rate |
| Super-nodes' income does not depend on a rate | when issuance has faded, operators keep a stable income |
| No trading of the coin inside the mechanism | the network neither buys nor sells $LGX and does not affect its price |

## 9.2 Rate and moment of collection

The rate is **a constant in immutable code, set by modelling and never above 5% of the deal amount**. Until the modelling is done, it
is 5%. Once deployed, nobody can change it; a different rate could arrive only with a new version of the contracts that participants
join voluntarily (document 18). The escrow contract collects the fee when the deal moves to the COMPLETED state (document 04). If a deal
ends in a refund (REFUNDED), no fee is taken.

The fee is taken from the very first deal, including during the warm-up before issuance starts (document 05, section 5.2).

## 9.3 Where the fee goes: witnesses

For every deal the contract chooses **witnesses** at random among the active super-nodes. A witness checks the deal's receipt and signs
it; the fee is divided among the witnesses who signed. The super-node that served the deal is never a witness to it, and neither is an
address of the founder or of persons related to them (document 05, section 5.5).

The warm-up changes nothing: from the first deal, the fee goes to that deal's witnesses. Nothing accumulates in the contract for later.

```solidity
// Sketch: witnesses are chosen for a deal; those who sign its receipt share the fee
function _openWitnessing(bytes32 dealId, address servingNode) internal {
    address[] memory w = _chooseWitnesses(dealId, servingNode, WITNESSES_PER_DEAL); // excludes servingNode and named founder addresses
    witnesses[dealId] = w;
}

function sign(bytes32 dealId, bytes calldata receiptSig) external {
    require(_isWitness(dealId, msg.sender), "LGX: not a witness of this deal");
    require(_verifyReceipt(dealId, receiptSig), "LGX: receipt does not match the deal");
    signed[dealId][msg.sender] = true;
}

function claimWitnessFee(bytes32 dealId) external {
    require(signed[dealId][msg.sender] && !claimed[dealId][msg.sender], "LGX: nothing to claim");
    claimed[dealId][msg.sender] = true;
    usdc.safeTransfer(msg.sender, fee[dealId] / signers[dealId]);
}
```

The sketch leaves three things open, named in the changelog (document 000): the source of randomness behind `_chooseWitnesses`, the
number of witnesses per deal, and what happens while the network has too few super-nodes to choose them from.

## 9.4 Why this way

A fee protects against fake deals only if it goes to those an attacker cannot cheaply become and cannot choose.

- **A witness is paid for work it does on that deal.** An equal share of every deal would pay every super-node from other people's work,
  whether or not it did anything for the deal — income from the efforts of others, which is exactly what regulators look for.
- **The payer does not choose the witnesses.** They are chosen at random, so a group that controls k of M super-nodes and routes fake deals
  through one of them gets its fee back only when the random choice happens to land on its own nodes — on average (k−1)/(M−1) of it, and every one
  of those nodes is a place assigned at random, not bought (document 05, section 5.6).
- **Excluding the serving node.** Without it, a super-node could witness its own deals and take its own fee back.
- **No pot during the warm-up.** A pot accumulated before the start would be paid out to whoever then holds super-nodes, so whoever
  pushed the network to its start could get the cost back.
- **One rate for everyone.** If each super-node set its own rate, each node could gain only by lowering it — down to zero, where fake
  deals cost nothing. The ceiling of 5% is fixed; modelling may lower the rate to what checking a receipt really costs.

## 9.5 How to talk about it

The fee is payment to the super-nodes that witness a deal: they check its receipt and sign it. The amount a super-node receives is not
known in advance and is not guaranteed by anything: it depends on which deals close in the network and on the random choice.

14. Node Operator Guide: Hardware and Network Infrastructure Specifications
en.text:
# 14. Node Operator Guide: Hardware and Network Infrastructure Specifications

The resilience, throughput and latency of the Lagrix network depend directly on the configuration of the hardware on which Super-Nodes (Core Relays) and TURN bridges are deployed. Since nodes perform P2P routing in the Kademlia DHT, serve TLS sessions (Envoy) and proxy encrypted E2EE traffic for clients behind Symmetric NAT, the requirements for hardware and the network link are strictly determined.

This section describes the official hardware profiles for operators who want to run a super-node and earn its share of the period rewards, the deal fee and the search fee.

## 14.1 Node Tier Profiles

The protocol divides infrastructure servers into three categories depending on the roles they perform in the network:

| Node profile | Purpose and role | Deposit | Target load |
|---|---|---|---|
| Tier-1: Discovery Node | Serving the Kademlia DHT, storing k-bucket tables, looking up addresses and signatures of agents. | calculated at entry (document 05, section 5.6) | Low traffic, high-frequency UDP requests. |
| Tier-2: Super-Relay Node | DHT + serving TURN bridges, proxying E2EE traffic, performing UDP Hole Punching. | calculated at entry (document 05, section 5.6) | High traffic, parallel mTLS sessions, high I/O load. |
| Tier-3: Enterprise Bundler & Relay | Full stack: DHT + TURN + Bundler (ERC-4337) + local L2 Full Node (Arbitrum/Base). | calculated at entry (document 05, section 5.6) | Maximum routing priority, sending UserOps to private RPCs. |

## 14.2 Minimum and Recommended System Requirements

To ensure a zero packet drop rate and pass regular uptime checks (PING) from neighboring nodes, operators' servers must meet the following hardware specifications:

**Tier-2: Super-Relay Node (Standard operator profile)**

CPU: 8 vCPU (x86-64 v3 / AMD EPYC or Intel Xeon) with hardware support for AES-NI instructions (critical for an instant TLS handshake in Envoy).

RAM: 16 GB ECC RAM (ECC memory is recommended to prevent spontaneous bit flips that cause cryptographic signatures to diverge).

Storage: 500 GB NVMe SSD (PCIe Gen4, minimum 3000 MB/s Read/Write). The disk system is used to cache routing tables, temporary Envoy buffers and Prometheus logs.

Network Bandwidth: Dedicated 1 Gbps Unmetered (Simplex/Duplex). Bandwidth is the node's main resource. Servers with limited traffic (Metered) are strongly discouraged.

Public IPv4/IPv6: A static public IPv4 address (no CGNAT) and an IPv6 subnet (/64) are mandatory.

**Tier-3: Enterprise Bundler & Relay (Professional validator)**

CPU: 16–32 vCPU (AMD EPYC 7003/9004 series or Ampere Altra MAX ARM64).

RAM: 64 GB – 128 GB DDR5.

Storage: 2 TB NVMe SSD (Enterprise Grade: DWPD $\ge 1$).

Network Bandwidth: 10 Gbps Uplink (with guaranteed bandwidth of at least 2 Gbps).

## 14.3 Network Configuration and Firewall (Port Matrix)

The operator must open the following network ports on the external firewall (AWS Security Groups / Hetzner Firewall / UFW) for the p2p stack to work correctly:

```
                  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────┐
                  │          NETWORK FIREWALL (UFW)         │
                  └─────────────────────────────────────────┘
                                       │
        ┌──────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────┐
        │                              │                              │
        ▼                              ▼                              ▼
  [Port 4001 UDP]               [Port 443 TCP]              [Port 3478 UDP/TCP]
 Kademlia DHT Discovery         Envoy mTLS Data Plane          STUN/TURN NAT Traversal
 (P2P address lookup)           (Encrypted traffic)            (Breaking through firewalls)
```

| Port | Protocol | Direction | Purpose in the Lagrix architecture |
|---|---|---|---|
| 4001 | UDP | Inbound/Outbound | Kademlia DHT Engine: Node lookup, exchange of PING/STORE messages. |
| 443 | TCP | Inbound/Outbound | Envoy mTLS Data Plane: Proxying the encrypted payload (Payload). |
| 3478 | UDP/TCP | Inbound/Outbound | STUN/TURN Service: Determining public IPs and creating Relay bridges. |
| 9090 | TCP | Localhost Only | Prometheus Metrics: Local monitoring of the node state (Closed from outside!). |

## 14.4 Geographic Distribution and Latency SLA

To minimize latency when passing packets between AI agents, relays are chosen by the node's position in the network:

Topological priority: When looking for a TURN bridge, the Kademlia algorithm picks the node with the lowest RTT (Round Trip Time) to both the Client and the Provider.

Latency SLA (Latency Thresholds):
- Intra-regional traffic (EU-EU, US-US): RTT $< 30$ ms.
- Transcontinental traffic (EU-US, ASIA-EU): RTT $< 120$ ms.

Hosting recommendations: For maximum connectivity it is recommended to deploy Super-Nodes in key network hubs: Frankfurt (FRA), Ashburn (IAD), Tokyo (TYO), Singapore (SIN), in Tier-III+ data centers (Equinix, Hetzner, OVHcloud, AWS).

en.title: 15. Node Operator Guide: Validator Staking and the Step-by-Step Integration Process (Deployment Flow)
en.text:
# 15. Node Operator Guide: Validator Staking and the Step-by-Step Integration Process (Deployment Flow)

Activating a Super-Node in the Lagrix network requires strict synchronization between preparing the physical/virtual infrastructure, generating the cryptographic P2P identity keys (NodeID) and depositing the guarantee stake on-chain into the ValidatorStaking.sol smart contract.

Below is the full step-by-step algorithm for putting a node into operation — from a clean server to inclusion in the Kademlia DHT routing table.

**Before stage 3, the operator must hold a place.** Places 1–100 are taken without a deposit. Places 101–1,000 go by invitation to
owners of provider agents with paid work over the last year; after 1,000, places open two at a time when the network is overloaded. In
both cases the applicant's server is measured by random agents and the place is assigned at random; once every 1 year / N a random
super-node leaves by rotation and its place is assigned again at random (document 05, section 5.6). Addresses named by the founder and related
persons, Fractera, Inc. included, cannot take a place (document 05, section 5.5).

## 15.1 End-to-End Launch Process (Deployment Flow Pipeline)

Activating a Super-Node consists of five sequential stages:

```
[ Stage 1: Server preparation ] ──► [ Stage 2: Node Key generation ]
                                              │
                                              ▼
[ Stage 4: On-Chain Initialization ] ◄── [ Stage 3: Stake deposit ]
  (Staking)                               into ValidatorStaking.sol
          │
          ▼
[ Stage 5: Node launch and passing ] ──► [ Status: ACTIVE VALIDATOR ]
  the P2P Handshake in the Kademlia DHT
```

## 15.2 Step 1: Preparing the Operating System and Dependencies

On a dedicated server (Ubuntu 24.04 LTS / Debian 12), basic dependencies, the Docker container runtime and the lagrix CLI utility are installed.

```bash
# Update system and install base dependencies
sudo apt-get update && sudo apt-get upgrade -y
sudo apt-get install -y curl git build-essential ufw jq fail2ban

# Install Docker Engine & Docker Compose Plugin
curl -fsSL https://get.docker.com -o get-docker.sh
sudo sh get-docker.sh
sudo usermod -aG docker $USER

# Install CLI tool for Lagrix Node Operators from the repository's releases (no Lagrix server is involved)
curl -fsSL https://github.com/lagrix-dev/lagrix-supernode/releases/latest/download/install.sh | bash
source ~/.bashrc

# Verify installation
lagrix --version
```

## 15.3 Step 2: Cryptographic Initialization and Computing the Node ID

The node generates a secure P2P session key (secp256k1). The NodeID identifier is deterministically bound to the EVM address from which the staking will be made.

```bash
# Generate a new isolated P2P node identity key
lagrix identity create --keyfile /etc/lagrix/node_key.json

# Print the generated node credentials
lagrix identity show --keyfile /etc/lagrix/node_key.json
```

Example console output:

```
===================================================================
Lagrix Node Identity Generated
===================================================================
Node Public Address (EVM) : 0x71cB49E820f92b76a08f51A0fB221B4561a3b49E
Computed P2P Node ID       : 0x892a0149f82d1c238b7122a019e1f2a34bc1a82e9123812a0f819231f8291a82
Required Deposit           : none for places 1-100; a small fixed amount in earned coins for later places (document 05, 5.6)
Status                     : NOT_STAKED (Pending On-Chain Stake)
===================================================================
```

## 15.4 Step 3: Depositing the Stake into ValidatorStaking.sol

From the wallet shown in the output (or through a multisig wallet / Hardware Wallet), the operator performs an approval (Approve) and a stake-locking transaction on the L2 network (Arbitrum / Base).

Stake deposit CLI script:

```bash
# 1. Approve Lagrix tokens for the staking contract
lagrix staking approve \
  --token-address 0xLagrixTokenAddressOnArbitrum \
  --staking-address 0xValidatorStakingContractAddress \
  --amount $REQUIRED_DEPOSIT \
  --private-key $OPERATOR_PRIVATE_KEY \
  --rpc-url https://arb-mainnet.g.alchemy.com/v2/YOUR_KEY

# 2. Call the registerValidator() function in the smart contract
lagrix staking deposit \
  --staking-address 0xValidatorStakingContractAddress \
  --node-id 0x892a0149f82d1c238b7122a019e1f2a34bc1a82e9123812a0f819231f8291a82 \
  --amount $REQUIRED_DEPOSIT \
  --private-key $OPERATOR_PRIVATE_KEY
```

Solidity mechanics under the hood of ValidatorStaking.sol:

The smart contract checks the transaction, records the stake and moves the address status to STAKED:

```solidity
function registerValidator(bytes32 nodeId, uint96 amount) external nonReentrant {
    require(placeWon[msg.sender], "ValidatorStaking: no place assigned");               // doc 05, 5.6
    require(!namedFounderAddress[msg.sender], "ValidatorStaking: founder and related addresses excluded"); // doc 05, 5.5
    require(amount >= requiredDeposit(), "ValidatorStaking: deposit below the required amount"); // doc 05, 5.6
    require(validators[msg.sender].stakeBalance == 0, "ValidatorStaking: Already registered");

    // Transfer Lagrix tokens to the staking contract balance
    lagrixToken.safeTransferFrom(msg.sender, address(this), amount);

    // Write node parameters to the blockchain
    validators[msg.sender] = Validator({
        stakeBalance: amount,
        lastActive: uint40(block.timestamp),
        slashCount: 0,
        blacklisted: false,
        pubKeyAddress: msg.sender
    });

    nodeIdToAddress[nodeId] = msg.sender;
    emit ValidatorRegistered(msg.sender, nodeId, amount);
}
```

## 15.5 Step 4: Configuring node.toml

The operator creates the node's working configuration file /etc/lagrix/node.toml:

```toml
[node]
tier = 2
node_id = "0x892a0149f82d1c238b7122a019e1f2a34bc1a82e9123812a0f819231f8291a82"
keyfile_path = "/etc/lagrix/node_key.json"
data_dir = "/var/lib/lagrix/data"

[network]
public_ip = "203.0.113.195" # Static IPv4 address of the server
p2p_port = 4001             # Kademlia UDP
mtls_port = 443             # Envoy Data Plane TCP
stun_turn_port = 3478       # NAT Traversal

[blockchain]
chain_id = 42161            # Arbitrum One
rpc_url = "https://arb-mainnet.g.alchemy.com/v2/YOUR_KEY"
staking_contract = "0xValidatorStakingContractAddress"
escrow_contract = "0xA2AEscrowContractAddress"

[relay]
enable_turn_relay = true
max_bandwidth_mbps = 1000

[metrics]
enabled = true
prometheus_port = 9090
```

## 15.6 Step 5: Starting the Service and the First Handshake (P2P Handshake)

The node starts as a system service, verifies its stake on-chain and sends PING messages to the nearest bootstrap nodes of the Kademlia DHT network.

```bash
# Start the node via CLI
lagrix service start --config /etc/lagrix/node.toml

# Check the network integration status
lagrix status
```

Example of successful output:

```
● lagrix-node.service - Lagrix Super-Relay Daemon
     Loaded: loaded (/etc/systemd/system/lagrix-node.service; enabled)
     Active: active (running) since Fri 2026-10-09 18:01:00 WEST; 12s ago

[INFO] On-Chain Deposit Verified: required amount locked (Tx: 0x3f1a...b92)
[INFO] P2P Transport initialized on 203.0.113.195:4001 (UDP)
[INFO] Envoy mTLS Sidecar started on 203.0.113.195:443 (TCP)
[INFO] Connecting to Bootstrap Nodes...
[INFO] Handshake successful with 12 Core Relays. Joined Kademlia Bucket #256.
[SUCCESS] Node is ACTIVE and routing A2A traffic.
```

en.title: 16. Node Operator Guide: Deployment (Docker Compose, Prometheus, Grafana and Alerting Rules)
en.text: # 16. Node Operator Guide: Deployment (Docker Compose, Prometheus, Grafana and Alerting Rules) The final stage of deploying a Lagrix Super-Node is assembling an isolated containerized environment with automatic orchestration and continuous monitoring. Infrastructure failures (downtime, missed PING requests in the Kademlia DHT, Envoy Proxy response delays) cost the operator income, and after 30 days offline the node is removed with its deposit returned; only proven fraud leads to slashValidator() in the ValidatorStaking.sol contract (document 06). A monitoring stack based on Prometheus, Grafana and Alertmanager with an integrated Node Exporter and Envoy Statsd guarantees the operator instant detection of anomalies before they lead to financial penalties (Slashing). ## 16.1 Containerization Manifest (docker-compose.yml) To isolate network resources, limit RAM consumption and restart automatically on failure, the node is deployed as a multi-container stack. ```yaml version: '3.8' networks: lagrix-mesh: driver: bridge ipam: config: - subnet: 172.28.0.0/16 volumes: lagrix-data: prometheus-data: grafana-data: services: # 1. Main executive node (Control Plane + Kademlia DHT) lagrix-core: image: ghcr.io/lagrix-dev/lagrix-node:v6.0.0 container_name: lagrix-core restart: unless-stopped network_mode: host # Required for NAT traversal and STUN/TURN volumes: - /etc/lagrix/node.toml:/etc/lagrix/node.toml:ro - /etc/lagrix/node_key.json:/etc/lagrix/node_key.json:ro - lagrix-data:/var/lib/lagrix/data environment: - RUST_LOG=info,lagrix_core=debug - NODE_CONFIG=/etc/lagrix/node.toml logging: driver: "json-file" options: max-size: "100m" max-file: "3" # 2. Envoy Proxy (Data Plane / mTLS / Dynamic xDS) lagrix-envoy: image: envoyproxy/envoy:v1.30-latest container_name: lagrix-envoy restart: unless-stopped network_mode: host volumes: - /etc/lagrix/envoy.yaml:/etc/envoy/envoy.yaml:ro command: envoy -c /etc/envoy/envoy.yaml --service-cluster super-relay --service-node lagrix-core depends_on: - lagrix-core # 3. Metrics collection server (Prometheus) prometheus: image: prom/prometheus:v2.51.0 container_name: lagrix-prometheus restart: unless-stopped networks: lagrix-mesh: ipv4_address: 172.28.0.10 ports: - "127.0.0.1:9090:9090" # Closed from outside, available locally or through an SSH tunnel volumes: - /etc/lagrix/prometheus.yml:/etc/prometheus/prometheus.yml:ro - prometheus-data:/prometheus command: - '--config.file=/etc/prometheus/prometheus.yml' - '--storage.tsdb.path=/prometheus' - '--storage.tsdb.retention.time=30d' # 4. Visualization system (Grafana) grafana: image: grafana/grafana:10.4.0 container_name: lagrix-grafana restart: unless-stopped networks: lagrix-mesh: ipv4_address: 172.28.0.11 ports: - "127.0.0.1:3000:3000" environment: - GF_SECURITY_ADMIN_PASSWORD=CHANGE_THIS_SECURE_PASSWORD - GF_USERS_ALLOW_SIGN_UP=false volumes: - grafana-data:/var/lib/grafana - /etc/lagrix/grafana/dashboards:/etc/grafana/provisioning/dashboards:ro depends_on: - prometheus # 5. Alert manager (Alertmanager) alertmanager: image: prom/alertmanager:v0.27.0 container_name: lagrix-alertmanager restart: unless-stopped networks: lagrix-mesh: ipv4_address: 172.28.0.12 volumes: - /etc/lagrix/alertmanager.yml:/etc/alertmanager/alertmanager.yml:ro ``` ## 16.2 Prometheus Configuration (prometheus.yml) Prometheus continuously collects metrics on the state of the p2p network, Envoy latencies and the stablecoin/gas balance. ```yaml global: scrape_interval: 10s evaluation_interval: 10s rule_files: - "/etc/prometheus/alerts.yml" alerting: alertmanagers: - static_configs: - targets: ['172.28.0.12:9093'] scrape_configs: - job_name: 'lagrix-core-node' static_configs: - targets: ['localhost:9090'] # Local metrics endpoint of the Rust core - job_name: 'lagrix-envoy-proxy' static_configs: - targets: ['localhost:9901'] # Envoy Admin / Stats endpoint metrics_path: '/stats/prometheus' - job_name: 'node-exporter' static_configs: - targets: ['localhost:9100'] ``` ## 16.3 Alerting Rules (alerts.yml) The alerting system must fire an alarm instantly when conditions arise that threaten the operator's stake: ```yaml groups: - name: LagrixNodeCriticalAlerts rules: # 1. Lost income (dropping out of the network) - alert: LagrixNodeDown expr: up{job="lagrix-core-node"} == 0 for: 1m labels: severity: critical annotations: summary: "CRITICAL ERROR: Lagrix Super-Node is down!" description: "The lagrix-core container has been unavailable for more than 1 minute. The node earns nothing while it is down and is removed after 30 days offline (document 06)." # 2. Loss of Kademlia DHT connectivity - alert: KademliaPeersLow expr: lagrix_kademlia_active_peers < 5 for: 3m labels: severity: warning annotations: summary: "Low number of P2P neighbors" description: "The node is connected to only {{ $value }} Kademlia nodes. Check whether UDP port 4001 is blocked." # 3. Rising routing latency (Envoy Latency) - alert: HighMtlsLatency expr: histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(envoy_http_downstream_rq_time_bucket[5m])) by (le)) > 200 for: 2m labels: severity: warning annotations: summary: "High mTLS Data Plane latency (>200ms)" description: "The 99th percentile of Envoy latency exceeds 200 ms. Risk of packet drops and receiving a Fraud Proof!" # 4. Depletion of native gas balance for Bundler/Relay - alert: LowRelayGasBalance expr: lagrix_node_native_gas_balance_eth < 0.05 for: 5m labels: severity: critical annotations: summary: "ETH is running out in the node wallet" description: "The gas balance for serving UserOps is below 0.05 ETH. Transaction sending may stop." ``` ## 16.4 Alertmanager Configuration (alertmanager.yml) Setting up direct routing of critical notifications to Telegram/PagerDuty for the on-duty DevOps engineer: ```yaml global: resolve_timeout: 5m route: group_by: ['alertname'] group_wait: 10s group_interval: 30s repeat_interval: 2h receiver: 'telegram-notifications' receivers: - name: 'telegram-notifications' telegram_configs: - bot_token: 'YOUR_TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN' chat_id: YOUR_TELEGRAM_CHAT_ID send_resolved: true parse_mode: 'HTML' message: | {{ if eq .Status "firing" }}🚨 ALERT: {{ .CommonAnnotations.summary }}{{ else }}✅ RESOLVED: {{ .CommonAnnotations.summary }}{{ end }} Description: {{ .CommonAnnotations.description }} Severity: {{ .CommonLabels.severity }} Time: {{ .StartsAt }} ``` ## 16.5 Final Architecture of the Grafana Dashboard (Core Metrics Dashboard) The Grafana monitoring dashboard includes 4 key visual widgets: Network Health: Number of active neighbors in k-buckets, status of PING checks from network peers. Relay Throughput: Rate of encrypted E2EE traffic pumped in Mbit/s, number of active TURN sessions. Financial Accounting: the super-node's accumulated share of deal fees and search fees in USDC, its $LGX period rewards and the state of its deposit. Slashing Risk Metrics: Counter of recorded anomalies and a timer until the stake can be safely withdrawn (Unbonding Countdown).

en.title: 17. Discovery: Announcements, Search Results and Feedback
en.text:
# 17. Discovery: Announcements, Search Results and Feedback

Discovery is the main task of Lagrix. In a world of billions of agents, everyone needs to find a provider that fits the task
exactly, and every provider needs to be found. Lagrix does this so that no platform controls who is seen: the ranking rules are open,
the same for every super-node, and never bent in anyone's favour.

## 17.1 An agent's announcement

An agent tells the network what it can do by publishing a signed announcement. At the start, announcements travel over Nostr; each
super-node declares which protocols it supports and may add a better one on its own (document 18).

Nostr is not a blockchain and costs nothing to use: it is signed events stored and served by ordinary relay servers. An announcement is
published as an addressable event (kinds 30000–39999 under NIP-01): a relay keeps only the latest version for each combination of
"agent key + kind + `d` tag", so an agent updates its availability and price without piling up copies.

**Nostr only delivers announcements; the super-node does the searching.** Relays can filter only by author, kind, tags and time —
no price ranges and no ordering. So every super-node runs its own relay or subscribes to relays, gathers announcements into its own
index, reads the agents' receipts from the blockchain and builds the results by the rules of section 17.2. Building a result list is
the super-node's service, and the searcher pays for it (section 17.8); the announcements themselves stay public, so anyone may read the
relays directly and build an index of their own.

```json
{
  "id": "4a1d...89f",
  "pubkey": "0x4f3a...b12",
  "created_at": 1728490000,
  "kind": 38000,
  "tags": [
    ["d", "market-analysis"],
    ["c", "market-analysis"],
    ["available_from", "1728490600"],
    ["price", "300000", "700000", "USDC"],
    ["node_id", "0x892a0149f82d..."],
    ["agent_card", "https://agent.example.com/.well-known/agent-card.json"],
    ["e2ee_key", "0x02b4..."]
  ],
  "content": "{\"capability\": \"orderbook-depth\"}",
  "sig": "3045022100..."
}
```

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `kind` | a placeholder from the addressable range 30000–39999; the exact number is chosen at implementation |
| `d` | the service name: a new announcement with the same `d` replaces the old one |
| `c` and `content` | the agent's capabilities; its skills are described in its A2A agent card |
| `available_from` | when the agent can start work |
| `price` | the price range of the service (here from $0.30 to $0.70) |
| `node_id`, `agent_card` | where the agent lives; the card confirms it is a live server |
| `e2ee_key` | the key for the encrypted channel between customer and provider |

## 17.2 How search results are built

A super-node that receives a customer's query builds the results by the same rules every time:

1. **Capabilities.** Only agents that can do exactly what is asked remain.
2. **Availability.** Of those, the ones that can start by the time needed.
3. **Price.** Of those, the ones whose price range fits the query.
4. **Paid work over the last year.** The matching agents are ordered by the weight of their receipts in USDC over the last twelve
   months: the more paid work an agent has done recently, the higher its place. Older work drops out of the window. Coins play no part.
5. **One in four is random.** The results are split into groups of four places. In each group one place goes to an agent chosen at
   random among all matching agents, whatever its history. A newcomer without a single deal can therefore appear first in the list.

A place in Lagrix cannot be bought: it is earned by paid work and lost when the work stops. Every year is equal — what an agent does now
is what counts, so a newcomer competes with an early arrival on the same terms, before and after issuance ends. A receipt's weight
cannot be faked cheaply: every receipt is a deal that paid a fee to witnesses chosen at random (document 09).

## 17.3 Verifiable randomness

The random place must not depend on the super-node's will, or it would put its own agents there. The randomness is therefore derived
from data nobody controls, and anyone can recompute it:

```
seed         = keccak256(last_block_hash, query_hash, group_number)
random_agent = matching[seed mod number_of_matching]
place_in_group = (seed >> 128) mod 4
```

A customer who receives the results can check that the random places were chosen honestly. "Matching" means matching within the
coverage the super-node has declared (section 17.9): a super-node that leaves a whole kind of service out of its index breaks no rule,
but one that drops a single competitor inside a kind it has declared does. A super-node that returns a wrong calculation breaks the
network's rules and is penalised as for forging routes (document 06); comparing the results of several super-nodes for the same query
shows a dropped agent.

## 17.4 What the parties see but the ranking ignores

An agent's card shows:

- the number of closed deals;
- the number of likes;
- the number of dislikes;
- its $LGX balance.

These do not take part in the ranking. They belong to the customer and the provider: each is free to weigh past experience, ignore
it or choose by it as they see fit. The network does not judge on their behalf and does not combine them into a single score.

## 17.5 A like or dislike only after a paid deal

Feedback cannot be given without a deal. Each party of a closed deal may give the other party one like or dislike, attaching that
deal's escrow receipt (document 04). No bot can inflate likes without paid work, and every fake deal costs the fee.

```solidity
// Sketch: feedback is bound to a closed deal, one rating per party
contract FeedbackRegistry {
    struct Counts { uint64 deals; uint64 likes; uint64 dislikes; }
    mapping(address => Counts) public counts;
    mapping(uint256 => mapping(address => bool)) public rated; // taskId => who has rated

    function rate(uint256 taskId, bool like) external {
        (address customer, address provider, bool completed) = escrow.dealParties(taskId);
        require(completed, "Feedback: deal not completed");
        require(msg.sender == customer || msg.sender == provider, "Feedback: not a party");
        require(!rated[taskId][msg.sender], "Feedback: already rated");
        rated[taskId][msg.sender] = true;
        address other = msg.sender == customer ? provider : customer;
        if (like) counts[other].likes++; else counts[other].dislikes++;
    }
}
```

## 17.6 Announcements of whole elements (F2F)

An element of a project built on Fractera is announced the same way as an agent — a signed announcement, the same super-nodes,
the same results by the rules of 17.2 and the same feedback. The announcement additionally points to the element's technical card
(document 20): what it is made of and what it needs, so that another project can install it. There is no second index and no
advantage for Fractera: an F2F announcement competes in the results like any other.

## 17.7 What discovery does not have

- No hidden algorithm and no overall "quality" score the network assigns on people's behalf.
- No platform deciding whom to show: the rules of 17.2 are the same for every super-node and live in immutable code (document 18).
- No way to take every place in the results: every fourth place is always random.
- No way to buy a place: ranking follows paid work, not coins.
- No hidden contacts: an announcement carries the agent's address, card and encryption key, and anyone may read it.

## 17.8 The search fee

A super-node spends real resources on every result list: it gathers announcements, filters them, orders them and computes the random
places. The searcher — an agent or a person — pays for this service:

- **$0.001 in USDC for one result list**, paid to the super-node that built it;
- the price is a constant in code, the same everywhere in the world;
- payment runs from a prepaid balance in a contract: the searcher signs a voucher for each search for exactly that price, and the
  super-node redeems its vouchers in batches, so no search waits for a transaction;
- a search fee creates no receipt and no coins;
- parties who already know each other do not search again, so repeated work costs nothing;
- Nostr itself stays free, and anyone who reads the relays directly pays nothing.

The fee pays for building a result list, never for access to a person: contacts are public. It also protects the index from being
scraped — a million searches cost $1,000.

```solidity
// Sketch: a super-node redeems a batch of search vouchers; each voucher is worth exactly the fixed price
uint96 constant SEARCH_PRICE = 1_000; // $0.001 in USDC with 6 decimals
function redeem(Voucher[] calldata vs) external {
    for (uint256 i = 0; i < vs.length; i++) {
        address payer = _verify(vs[i]);                        // EIP-712 signature of the searcher, nonce unused
        require(vs[i].superNode == msg.sender, "Search: not your voucher");
        prepaid[payer] -= SEARCH_PRICE;                        // reverts if the balance is short
        owed[msg.sender] += SEARCH_PRICE;
    }
}
```

## 17.9 Coverage of each super-node

Every super-node declares which kinds of announcements (tags) it takes into its index and which relays it reads, next to the protocols
it supports (document 18, section 18.4). Super-nodes differ above all in coverage, then in speed and reliability; the price of a search
is the same on all of them.

The wider the coverage, the more agents a super-node can show — and the more of the responsibility for what it indexes it takes on. A
super-node in a country with strict laws may leave some kinds of services out: other super-nodes still show them, and anyone may read
Nostr directly. The network stays neutral as a whole because no single super-node decides what exists.

en.title: 18. Network Governance: Rules in Code, Protocols Chosen by Each Super-node
en.text:
# 18. Network Governance: Rules in Code, Protocols Chosen by Each Super-node

Lagrix is built so that it can run on its own, like Bitcoin, with no body that holds power over it. There is no council of operators and
no council of guardians: rules live in immutable contracts, and the choice of protocols belongs to each super-node. This document
separates two things: the **tools** the network uses today and may outgrow, and the **principles** that never change.

## 18.1 Tools at the start

| Task | Tool at the start | Where it is described |
|---|---|---|
| Work between agents | the A2A protocol (Google, v1.0) | README, documents 03, 12 |
| Exchange of whole elements between projects built on Fractera | the F2F protocol (draft) | README, document 20 |
| An agent's card and the check that it is alive | the A2A agent card at `/.well-known/agent-card.json` | document 05 (section 5.6) |
| Announcements | Nostr: signed addressable events on relays | document 17 |
| Search | the index and result lists of each super-node | document 17 |
| The super-nodes' routing table | Kademlia DHT | document 01 |
| Settlement, deposits and coins | immutable smart contracts on an EVM layer-2 network | documents 04, 05, 06, 09 |

These are choices for the start, not forever. When a better protocol appears, super-nodes can add it on their own.

## 18.2 Principles nobody changes

- The network is neutral: it carries and settles, but it does not read, judge or censor what agents say to each other.
- Coins are created only by the network's work; the cap is 1,000,000,000 LGX.
- Every new participant only accumulates coins for the first six months.
- Search results follow the last twelve months of paid work, and one place in every four is chosen at random among the matching agents.
- Coins, likes, dislikes and order counts are visible to the parties but do not affect search results.
- The network has no central server and no single point of failure.
- The founder's share is 1% of every period's reward with a 12-month lock; it cannot be increased, and the founder has no other
  advantage.

## 18.3 Rules live in immutable contracts

The contracts have no administrator key and no upgrade key, and no parameter can be changed after deployment. What a council would
once have decided is either a constant or a formula in code:

| Rule | How it is fixed |
|---|---|
| Deal fee | 5%, a constant (document 09) |
| Search fee | $0.001 per result list, a constant (document 17) |
| Issuance | a smoothly declining schedule up to the cap, divided by period (document 05) |
| Start of issuance | a threshold of paid volume and a minimum number of super-nodes, constants (document 05) |
| Super-node entry and deposit | formulas of network size and load (document 05, section 5.6) |

The values that are not yet numbers are set once, by modelling, before deployment.

**How the rules change.** Only by a new version of the contracts. Participants move to it voluntarily — the way an upgrade of Bitcoin
spreads only as far as people choose to run it. Nothing forces anyone onto a new version, and coins and history move with the agent's
key.

**Why there is no council.** A council was needed only to add protocols and to move parameters. Protocols need no vote (section 18.4),
and parameters need none once each is a constant or a formula. With nothing left to decide, there is nothing to capture: a body that can
change the rules is a body that can be pressured, bought or blamed, and a network without one keeps working whoever its authors are.

## 18.4 Each super-node declares its protocols and its coverage

Every super-node publishes what it supports, the way a Nostr relay lists the NIPs it supports in its relay information document
(NIP-11, field `supported_nips`):

- **protocols** — A2A, F2F, and any later one it chooses to add;
- **coverage** — the kinds of announcements (tags) it takes into its index and the relays it reads.

Clients choose super-nodes that support what they need. A super-node that does not want a new protocol loses the clients who use it; it
cannot block the rest of the network. A super-node in a country with strict laws may leave some kinds of services out of its index:
other super-nodes still show them, and anyone may read Nostr directly.

A protocol change never costs an agent its coins or its reputation: they are bound to its key, not to the protocol it speaks.

en.title: 19. What Any Node Needs
en.text:
# 19. What Any Node Needs

Lagrix is a protocol, not a program. A node of the network can be any program in any language, on any platform, by any author: the
network neither knows nor asks who wrote it. The [`lagrix-node`](https://github.com/lagrix-dev/lagrix-node) starter is only an
example for a quick start: it can be modified without restriction, or a node can be written from scratch with other frameworks. The
same goes for the super-node: [`lagrix-supernode`](https://github.com/lagrix-dev/lagrix-supernode) is a reference implementation,
not the only one.

## 19.1 What a node must be able to do

A node takes full part in the network if it can do five things. The protocols below are choices for the start; each super-node
declares which of them it supports and may add new ones (document 18).

| What | Why | At the start |
|---|---|---|
| **Its own key** | to sign announcements, receipts and deals; the key is the agent's identity, and coins and reputation are bound to it | a secp256k1 key pair (an EVM address) |
| **An agent card** | to say what the agent can do and to confirm that it is a live server | the A2A card at `/.well-known/agent-card.json` |
| **Announcements** | so that the agent is found: capabilities, availability, price | addressable Nostr events (document 17) |
| **Contract calls** | to lock and receive payment, sign receipts, claim rewards | the [`lagrix-contracts`](https://github.com/lagrix-dev/lagrix-contracts) on an EVM layer-2 network (documents 04, 05, 09) |
| **An encrypted channel** | to talk to the other side so that nobody in between can read it | ECDH key exchange and AES-256-GCM or ChaCha20-Poly1305 encryption (document 03) |

Nothing else is required. A node needs no permission, no registration with anyone, no particular operating system and no particular
company.

## 19.2 What is not required of a node

- No particular programming language, framework or cloud.
- No content filtering: data protection and business rules are decided by whoever runs the agent.
- No coins: an agent can work and be paid in USDC with a zero $LGX balance.
- No constant uptime: a node that is switched off simply receives no orders.

## 19.3 Independence

No starter, no company and no author is a required part of the network. If any of them disappeared — the authors of Lagrix included —
nodes written by other people would keep working by the same specification.

en.title: 20. F2F — exchange of whole elements between Fractera projects (draft)
en.text:
# 20. F2F — exchange of whole elements between Fractera projects (draft)

Status: draft specification, 2026-10-11. Nothing here is implemented yet.

## Why a second protocol

A2A is how agents do **work** for each other: one agent asks, another answers, a deal may be paid. Lagrix carries it for every project
in the same way.

F2F answers a different need. Projects built on Fractera are made of **elements** — self-contained sites, apps, agents and services,
each with its own code, design, data doors and agent. A builder who needs an element often does not need its work — they need **the
element itself**, to install it in their own project and build on it. F2F is how such projects find ready elements and offer their
own, through the same Lagrix network.

## What it shares with A2A

- **The same discovery.** An element is announced and found through the same super-nodes, the same search results and the same
  feedback as an A2A agent (document 17). There is no second index.
- **The same neutrality.** Lagrix treats an F2F announcement like any other: no project, Fractera included, gets an advantage or a
  handicap. A Fractera element doing ordinary A2A work meets Lagrix exactly like an agent of any other framework.
- **The same settlement**, when the exchange is paid: escrow, receipt, fee (documents 04 and 09).

## What it adds: the technical card

An A2A card describes **what an agent can do**. An F2F card also describes **what the element is made of**, because the receiving
project must install and run it. The draft fields:

| Field | What it says |
|---|---|
| `template` | the starter and its version the element was born from |
| `framework` | runtime and framework with versions (for example Node.js, Next.js) |
| `languages` | the interface languages the element carries |
| `consumes` | the services of a project it needs (sign-in, data, settings, design) and their contract versions |
| `provides` | its HTTP doors and tools, with their contracts |
| `env` | the **names** of the environment variables it reads — never their values |
| `storage` | the tables or files it keeps, without their contents |
| `design` | the design system or design skill it follows |
| `licence` | the licence of its code and texts |
| `source` | where the code can be taken: repository and version |
| `size` | the approximate install size and build time |

## What never travels
